items.title: Why Are Canon Lenses White? The Science Behind the Sideline Icon
items.summary_what: Why Are Canon Lenses White? The Science Behind the Sideline Icon: When you head to a sporting event, you will inevitably see a sea of big white lenses.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.
items.summary_action: Verify regional pricing, eligibility terms, and expiry date via the official link before claiming.
items.raw_content: When you head to a sporting event, you will inevitably see a sea of big white lenses. For decades, it was Canon lenses 99% of the time. There were likely some people in marketing who were happy to see their lenses a different color than Nikon. Today? There are a lot of Sony lenses being used that also use their version of the white paint. Nikon has had a lens here or there, but all of their current lenses are black. Reverse marketing? So, while the white paint will always be part of Canon's branding, maybe less so today, there are real scientific reasons that Canon continues to evolve the white paint that most take for granted. Why Canon lenses are white is always one of the first questions budding photographers ask, and the simple answer is usually “to deal with heat.” That statement is true, but it's a bit more complex than that. The Problem with Sunshine Sometimes the sun can be a big problem for camera lenses. You will see accurate information out there about long lenses accentuating heatwaves, which is a regular occurrence for wildlife and outdoor sports photographers. Sometimes those heatwaves are from the environment; sometimes they can be from the heat coming off the lens itself. I think we all know that dark surfaces absorb light and turn it into heat, whereas lighter and whiter lenses reflect more light from the surface, reducing the impact of the heat generated. Conventional white Before 2018 Sunlight (infrared) Lens barrel ↑ Paint layer Titanium oxide (white pigment) Carbon black (tints the white) Carbon black soaks up infrared, so much of the sun's heat passes into the lens barrel. Heat-shield coating 2018 onward Sunlight (infrared) Lens barrel ↑ Paint layer Silica-coated titanium oxide Infrared-reflective pigment (replaces carbon black) Infrared is reflected away instead of absorbed, so far less heat reaches the barrel: 20% less temperature rise, according to Canon. Simplified illustration based on Canon Europe's description of the two paint formulations. Particle sizes and counts are not to scale. We call them white lenses, but they're a few shades off-white. If the lenses were pure white, you'd get some pretty nasty, bright reflections coming off the surface. Blinding yourself or the person beside you isn't the best thing. For the purpose of this exercise, we'll still call it “Canon White.” This coating has been 60 years in the making, and Canon continues to work to improve it. More Than 60 Years of White Canon first used a lighter color on its broadcast camera lenses in 1960, including the Canon TV 2000mm f/11 . The lens looked like 18% gray in color, and the signature “Canon White” would come about 15 years later. It wasn't until 1976 that Canon introduced white lenses to their SLR lineup. The goal was simple: reduce the heat on the surface of the lens to minimize thermal expansion and contraction. Canon TV 2000mm f/11 // Credit: Canon Inc. There was another big reason for the switch to reflective coatings for Canon: the proliferation of fluorite and synthetic fluorite elements. Fluorite is great at controlling chromatic aberrations, but it is more affected by heat than other glass element types. The white paint development was enough to keep the performance of the fluorite elements right where they wanted it to be. The Australian Open Problem It wasn't until the early 2000s that Canon realized what they had been doing with surface coatings wasn't enough and that it was time to make the white paint better. There were a lot of complaints from photographers using the EOS-1D at the Australian Open about autofocus performance issues. Canon tested the cameras and found nothing wrong with any of them. Canon sent a technician into the stands with the photographers to monitor the temperature of the cameras and lenses, and it turned out things were cooking. If you just lie on a lounger at the pool in 30°C weather under a high sun, most of us would feel a bit warm. That's what Canon discovered. Photographers aren't in the sun for half an hour; it can be an all-day affair. Canon had just discovered that too much heat was present inside the lens and that had effected the performance of the autofocus system. It was time to get back into R&D on the paint used for the surface of a camera lens barrel. The Sea of White // Credit: Canon Ireland Time for a New “Canon White” In 2018, Canon introduced a new heat-shield coating. The brief was demanding: the coating had to block more heat than ever, resist scratches and abrasion, avoid discoloring after long exposure to sunlight, feel good in the hand without being rough, and still look unmistakably like “Canon White.” This kind of technology can take a long time to develop, testing both optical performance in the field and the feasibility of manufacturing the coating in large quantities. Canon first looked at existing heat-shielding coatings, including ones used in the construction industry. None were tough enough. They couldn't handle the vibration and knocks a working lens takes, and a small bump could damage them. So, Canon decided to develop its own. What Changed? The original white paint got its shade by mixing white titanium oxide with carbon black. Carbon black is what absorbed infrared light. The new version swapped the carbon black for an infrared-reflective pigment, so sunlight’s infrared bounces off instead of soaking in. The titanium oxide is now also coated with silica. The new coating is more resistant to scratches and UV fading, too. As we know, it's not indestructible, and at some point, you're going to get one of those lovely chunks gouged out of the coating to expose the metal below. We like those battle scars around here, but not everyone does. The Shade of White Getting the right shade of white was a process. Engineers tested a pile of samples and spent time adjusting the shade, texture, the level of sheen, and even how much coating was applied to see what influence it had on the finished color and overall performance. In the end, Canon picked the color by eye because they couldn't quantify aesthetic outcomes with definitive data on the shade and application. Testing the performance was also a massive task. Canon engineers placed temperature sensors inside and outside the barrel, testing the old and new coatings side by side. They figured out that there were many slight variables with a direct impact on heat: things like small differences in the angle of the lens or whether or not there was a breeze. How much the new white helps Temperature rise of a lens in sunlight, conventional Canon white = 100 Conventional white paint titanium oxide + carbon black 100 Heat-shield coating (2018) silica-coated titanium oxide + IR-reflective pigment 80 −20% temperature rise Swapping the infrared-absorbing carbon black for an infrared-reflecting pigment means less of the sun's heat soaks into the lens. Source: Canon Europe. Canon quotes only the relative reduction, not absolute temperatures, so the bars are indexed rather than in °C. Through exhaustive testing, Canon concluded that the new coating reduced temperatures in the lens by about 20%. Does it Matter Today? Canon notes that modern RF lenses can be more prone to heat issues due to smaller barrel surface areas and fewer internal elements to distribute the heat load. Modern high-resolution image sensors can also reveal far more anomalies than film or early digital sensors. At 45MP, every atmospheric disturbance has a greater visual impact than on an older 12MP sensor. It’s similar to the days of mirror-slap on tripods: vibration blur was far more noticeable on a 50MP body than on a 24MP body. Lens Hoods Play a Role The coating on the lens hood plays a big role in battling the effects of heat. If the lens hood on a “Big White” were black, the front barrel would absorb heat directly at the entrance pupil, creating internal heat haze or a “mirage” effect inside the glass. So not only do lens hoods protect your glass from impacts and flare, they also play a critical role in keeping internal temperatures down. Keep in mind: the longer your focal length, the more exaggerated these heat-based anomalies become. Even on a smaller lens like the RF 100-500mm f/4.5-7.1L IS USM, which has far less surface area than an RF 600mm f/4L IS USM, the 500mm reach makes the heat-shield coating essential on both the barrel and hood. The coating debuted in 2018 on the EF 400mm f/2.8L IS III USM and EF 600mm f/4L IS III USM. The first RF lens to receive it was the RF 70-200mm f/2.8L IS USM in 2019, a compact zoom frequently relied upon by sports photographers under blazing summer heat. Canon White Through the Years More than 60 years of Canon white: why Canon's telephoto lenses are white, and how the paint went from a simple heat reflector to a purpose-built infrared-reflecting coating. 1960 Origin Broadcast lenses go white Canon first uses white on its broadcast camera lenses, including the TV2000mm F11. 1976 SLR era White comes to SLR lenses White is first used on Canon SLR lenses to reflect heat and minimise thermal expansion and contraction. That is especially important for heat-sensitive synthetic fluorite elements, which Canon pioneered in the 1960s. Early 2000s Field report The Australian Open problem Photographers shooting with the EOS-1D report autofocus problems. The cameras test fine, so a Canon technician sits with them and logs temperatures. The culprit turns out to be heat building up in lenses that sit in the sun for hours. 2018 Breakthrough New heat-shield coating Canon debuts its own coating on the EF 400mm f/2.8L IS III and EF 600mm f/4L IS III. It replaces IR-absorbing carbon black with an IR-reflective pigment and uses silica-coated titanium oxide, cutting temperature rise by 20% compared with the conventional paint. 2019 RF era First RF lens with the coating The RF 70-200mm F2.8 L IS USM becomes the first RF-mount lens to wear the new white, followed by the RF 70-200mm F4 L IS USM. Today Now Across the RF super-telephotos, and the hoods The coating is now used on lenses such as the RF 400mm F2.8, RF 600mm F4 and RF 100-500mm. It is also applied to their lens hoods, so a hot hood doesn't create heat haze inside the lens. Source: Canon and Canon Europe. The 20% figure is Canon's own comparison with its previous white paint. Why Aren't Smaller Lenses White? There are a few reasons why this paint color is saved for the bigger lenses. Smaller lenses have less surface area to soak up heat.. A lens like an RF 24-70mm f/2.8L IS USM isn't likely to be sitting baking in the sun on a tripod at an event. As mentioned earlier, the longer the focal length, the more likely you'll be able to see the negative effects of heat. Yes, there are the RF 100-400mm f/5.6-8 IS, RF 600mm f/11 and the RF 800mm f/11 black lenses in Canon's lineup, but they're not targeted at professionals who will be dealing with the sun for longer periods of time. Black is also better for videography to keep surface reflections to a minimum. Black is a bit more “stealth” when shooting events like a wedding. We imagine that the black coating is cheaper to use than the “Canon White” coating. In Closing The question of the white paint and why it exists has been asked for decades past and will be asked in the future, and for those of us that like to know why something is done the way it is, we think this topic will always be interesting. Canon could be working on the next iteration of this technology, as they seem to be a company that spends a lot of resources on the “little things”. Sure, one of those little things is going to be branding, but sometimes you get added benefits to advances in your technology. It has been 60 years of engineering just to try and keep the lenses cooler, and if they find a better way to do it, expect a new coating or two down the line.

items.title: Nikon Z5IIC review: an awkward viewfinderless camera design that’s heavy in the hand, heavy on specs, and light on your wallet

items.raw_content: The Nikon Z5IIC launched following rumors of a Nikon camera without a viewfinder. While there were whispers of a fixed-lens full-frame compact camera and a stills-focused Nikon ZR , nobody could have predicted a ‘viewfinderless’ clone of the Nikon Z5 II . Viewfinderless cameras have always been divisive. Photography purists cite the stability and sun-glare-free nature of shooting through the viewfinder as too crucial to pass up. But plenty of modern photographers ignore their EVF in favor of their mirrorless cameras’ rear LCD and a more dynamic method of shooting. What works for you, works. But the big question I’ll be trying to answer is what benefits the Nikon Z5IIC’s viewfinderless design brings to the table. One such benefit is price. With reports of the Nikon Z5 reaching the end of its lifecycle , the Nikon Z5IIC could soon become the most affordable entry point into Nikon’s full-frame mirrorless lineup at $1,399.95 / £1,349 / AU$2,399 (body only). And that entry point is exactly what Nikon is targeting. The ‘C’ in the camera’s name is supposed to represent ‘Casual’, which is why the Nikon Z5IIC is also the very first full-frame Z-series camera to feature Scene Modes. I took the Nikon Z5IIC for a spin around the beautiful city of Bath to find out how its viewfinderless design fared in a street photography setting. Read on for a deep dive into the camera’s specs and to find out how it performed in real-world scenarios. (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) Nikon Z5IIC vs Z5II: Specifications Nikon Z5IIC Nikon Z5 II Effective pixels 24.5MP BSI CMOS (full-frame) 24.5MP BSI CMOS (full-frame) ISO sensitivity Stills: 100–64000, (50-204,800 expanded) Video: 100–51200, Hi 2.0 Stills: 100–64000, (50-204,800 expanded) Video: 100–51200, Hi 2.0 Engine EXPEED 7 EXPEED 7 File format (Photo) RAW/JPEG/HEIF RAW/JPEG/HEIF Phase detection AF area Single-point AF: 273 points Auto-area AF: 299 points Single-point AF: 273 points Auto-area AF: 299 points Subject detection 10 types 9 types AF detection -10 EV -10EV Continuous shooting speed Electronic front-curtain shutter: 14 fps (CH+) Electronic shutter: 30 fps (C30) Electronic front-curtain shutter: 14 fps (CH+) Electronic shutter: 30 fps (C30) Vibration reduction 5-axis in-body VR: Up to 7.5 stops 5-axis in-body VR: Up to 7.5 stops Shutter speed 1/8000–30 sec (extendable up to 900 sec) 1/8000–30 sec (extendable up to 900 sec) Video frame size/frame rate 4K 60p (cropped) 4K 30p Full HD 120p 4K 60p (cropped) 4K 30p Full HD 120p Video compression N-RAW, H.265/264 N-RAW, H.265/264 Video recording mode N-Log, HLG, SDR N-Log, HLG, SDR Monitor 3.2-inch, approx. 1040k-dot vari-angle 3.2-inch, approx. 2100k-dot vari-angle Media slot SD (UHS-II) x1 SD (UHS-II) x2 Battery EN-EL15c (Rechargeable Li-ion) EN-EL15c (Rechargeable Li-ion) Dimensions (W×H×D) 5.3 x 3.3 x 2.9 in (134 × 80.5 × 72 mm) 5.3 x 4 x 2.9 in (134 x 100.5 x 72 mm) Weight (camera body only) 19 oz. / 538 g (body-only) 24.7 oz. / 620 g (body-only) Nikon Z5IIC: Price The Nikon Z5IIC is priced at $1,399.95 / £1,349 / AU$2,399 (body only). Compare that to the Nikon Z5 II , which is typically listed around $1,599 / £1,499 / AU$2,699, and that’s a decent saving of around $200 / £150 / AU$300. But one thing I’ve had in mind is where the Z5IIC will end up. As time goes on, we could see that body-only price creep towards the $1,000 mark. You can also opt to choose from various kits or bundles, such as the Nikon Z5IIC + Nikon Z 24-50mm f/4-6.3 ($1,699.95 / £1,609 / AU$2,949). This prime-sized zoom is a great choice for the camera’s viewfinderless design. While the Nikon Z5IIC + Nikon Z 24-200mm f/4-6.3 VR ($TBC / £2,049 / AU$3,699) might seem like a great all-in-one option, I’d be wary of any lens bigger than the Nikon Z 24-120mm f/4 S , which I used during my review. When you stack the Nikon Z5IIC against the Panasonic Lumix S9 and Sony A7C II , it’s priced between them. Overall, I think it’s competitively priced given its specs and the economic challenges the consumer tech industry is currently facing. Nikon Z5IIC: Design & Handling The Nikon Z5IIC largely follows the same formula as every other mainline Z-series camera: it’s solid, bulky, has a deep grip, and plenty of physical controls. The big difference is that it doesn’t have a faux pentaprism bump in which to house an electronic viewfinder. It’s less bulky and inherently more ‘riggable’ than any other full-frame Z-series camera (Nikon ZR aside). This allows it to occupy marginally less space in a backpack, weigh marginally less in the hand, look marginally less professional and intimidating, and cost marginally less than its blueprint, the Nikon Z5 II. The big question I had when using this camera was: Is ‘marginal’ enough to warrant the downgrade in functionality? I get it. Not every photographer wants to use a viewfinder, and there’s nothing wrong with that at all. If you’re prepared for bright, sunny conditions reflecting off the rear LCD and that doesn’t faze you, who am I to tell you otherwise? But the difference here is that the Nikon Z5IIC is a beefy, full-frame camera and that does change things. (Image credit: Mike Harris wearing a t-shirt and jeans holding the Nikon Z5IIC on a green background) Take the Panasonic Lumix S9 for example; a viewfinderless full-frame camera that’s roughly 135g lighter than the Nikon Z5IIC. That does make a difference. I’ve handed the Z5IIC off to various colleagues, and they’ve all been surprised by the same thing: its weight. The camera’s body weighs 538 g, which is a not-insignificant 82 g lighter than the Nikon Z5 II. And yet, the way you handle a viewfinderless camera is just different . Peer through a viewfinder and you’ll instinctively cradle a larger camera with both hands, but viewfinderless cameras need to be held farther from the body. The Z5IIC might be lighter than the Nikon Z5 II, but I noticed its weight more. That’s not to say the weight is a constant pain point, but it is a consideration. I used the camera with the Nikon Z 40mm f/2 and Nikon Z 24-120mm f/4 S. The latter is as heavy and bulky as I’d want to go for regular, handheld shooting. And even then, this is a relatively hefty setup for an everyday carry. (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) Use the Nikon Z5IIC for video, though, and the form factor isn’t an issue. Again, you tend to hold a camera differently when shooting video. Your forefinger doesn’t have to rest on the shutter button, meaning you can hold it in any way that feels comfortable to you. And of course, if you mainly shoot stills from a tripod, the form factor won’t be an issue at all, and most tripod users compose via the rear screen anyway. Ultimately, the lack of a viewfinder won’t be a turnoff for everyone, but the size and weight of the camera could be. I recommend trying it on for size in your local camera shop before buying, and considering very carefully what lenses you want to use with it. A telephoto-friendly camera this is not. A disappointing oversight from Nikon on paper is the Z5IIC’s rear screen. It’s actually lower resolution than the Nikon Z5II’s 2100k-dot screen (it’s 1040k dots). This really is a curious decision from Nikon and one that I can only assume was a budgetary measure. Still, you’d think the rear screen on a viewfinderless camera would be a core spec. And yet, despite my displeasure, if I’m going to be truly honest, I didn’t find this to be an issue out in the field. An oversight, yes, but not one that will impact the camera’s day-to-day usability. (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) Now that I’ve addressed the elephant in the room, let’s move on to some of the positives, of which there are plenty. As you’d expect from a mainline Z-series camera, the entire body feels solid. It’s built from magnesium alloy and durable-feeling plastics, while the grip is deep and covered in Nikon’s grippy leatherette. It’s also weather sealed, and while I’m not going to leave a $1399.95 / £1,349 camera out in a downpour, the UK’s dreadful weather meant I spent a lot of time using the Z5IIC in light showers. I never advise letting any camera get saturated, but I felt entirely confident using the Z5IIC in wet conditions. As per usual, Nikon has churned out a utilitarian device that’s built like a tank. But what’s unheard of from a mainline Z-series camera is that the Z5IIC comes in two colors. That’s right, it’s not just all-black with the classic red stripe; you can also opt for a silver variant. This paint job is only applied to the top plate, giving the camera a definite Sony A7C II vibe. Some of my colleagues think the silver looks plasticky, but as somebody who often moans about silver cameras looking cheap, I’d opt for the silver variant. Consider me a fan. (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) On the aforementioned top plate, you’ll find a fairly minimalist setup that’s functionally almost identical to the Nikon Z5 II. You’ve got a chunky mode dial that’s satisfyingly stiff, albeit slightly different to the Nikon Z5II’s in that it has only two U options instead of three. This is to facilitate the new Scene Mode icon (more on that later). Like the Z5 II, there’s also a very handy Picture Control button. Simply tap it and use the rear command dial to scroll through 31 ‘looks’ which are applied to images in real time. The left side of the top plate is typically bare, but without the viewfinder bump, it might have been nice to have included an ISO or exposure comp dial. Moving on to the rear, it’s standard fare except for the lack of a joystick. This is a real backwards step as far as I’m concerned. I can’t imagine it would have been an expensive addition. It simply means you’re forced to use the d-pad, which isn’t always as comfortable for your thumb, when holding the camera to accommodate its viewfinderless design. Thankfully, though, the buttons are solid and pleasantly spongy. Future / Mike Harris Future / Mike Harris Future / Mike Harris Future / Mike Harris Future / Mike Harris Future / Mike Harris The Nikon Z5IIC has a single SD-card slot, which is a downgrade from the Z5 II. However, this isn’t a pro-grade camera, and if you’re a stickler for pro features, you’re going to want a viewfinder anyway. As such, I think this is a sensible cost-saving measure that won’t bother most, especially with the ever-increasing price of memory cards these days. On the front of the camera, you’ve got two Fn buttons, which can be reached by extending your middle and forefinger from the grip, so they can be activated one-handed. And, like other Z-series cameras, the Z5IIC’s controls are highly customizable, so you can make the setup work for you. The camera uses Nikon’s standard EN-EL15c rechargeable Li-ion battery. According to the CIPA Shot Rating, it’s rated for 350 shots, which isn’t much different from the Nikon Z5II’s 330-380. During use, I can confirm that the battery held up as well as could be expected. Any concerns you might have about the rear LCD always being on can be easily dispelled. Firstly, by getting into the habit of switching your camera off when not in use. And secondly, by the fact that a standard mirrorless is constantly switching between an EVF and a rear LCD, the power usage isn’t going to be much different. Nikon Z5IIC: Performance Nikon’s second-generation Z-series lineup consists of the Nikon Z9 at the very top of the pyramid, with varying degrees of tech trickling down to other cameras in the range. As such, all of Nikon’s cameras boast very solid core performances and the Nikon Z5IIC is no different. In a world of high-megapixel sensors, you could look down upon the Z5IIC’s 24.5-MP sensor, but like all of Nikon’s full-frame image files, the stills you get from the Z5IIC really are top tier. RAW files stand up to generous cropping and are extremely pliable in post; they’re just an all-around treat to work with. And if editing RAW files isn’t your thing, the Nikon Z5IIC is loaded with Nikon’s Picture Controls. Think Fujifilm Film Simulations, but not as good fresh from the box. Thankfully, Picture Controls can be edited so you can come up with your own ‘recipes’, and you can even download examples from other creators. Film Grain isn’t simply overlaid onto your images; it’s rendered each time differently (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) A fairly recent update that debuted on the Nikon Zf is Film Grain. This complements Picture Controls by adding retro film grain to images. Not only does it look the part, but the grain isn’t uniform, so each application is different. I tested this myself and can confirm that it does indeed hold up to scrutiny. You can customize the grain by choosing from three different sizes and seven different intensities. I wouldn’t recommend using everything maxed out, but the default settings do look very convincing. Another feature that really lives up to the Nikon Z5IIC’s ‘Casual’ moniker is the presence of Scene Modes. The Z5IIC is the first full-frame Nikon camera to feature Scene Modes, and while that might not seem like a big deal, I think it’s a great addition. These modes are a great way for novice photographers to exercise a little creative agency beyond the one-size-fits-all Auto Mode. There are 15 Scene Modes in total, allowing you to adapt quickly to a variety of shooting situations. For example, I photographed my dog using the Pet Portraits Scene Mode. The camera instantly opened up the aperture and switched to Animal-Detection AF, so all I had to do was compose my image and fire the shutter. Think of Scene Modes as genre-specific automatic settings (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) Similarly, I tried out Night Landscape and Autumn Colors; the camera instantly adapted to both scenarios, raising the ISO and opening the aperture in low light, and warming the image and boosting the saturation when capturing autumnal foliage. Picture Controls and Scene modes aren’t for everyone, but I think they fit the Z5IIC’s intended demographic and are definite selling points for the right photographer. When it comes to autofocus, the Nikon Z5IIC performs very well. Sure, it can get a little stuck or confused at times, like any AF system, but provided you take the time to learn Nikon’s various modes, you’ll be well rewarded. I enjoy using 3D tracking, Wide-Area AF, and Single-Point AF, swapping between modes depending on the subject or scene at hand. I own a Nikon Z8, and while the Z8 will certainly perform better in a side-by-side comparison, I didn’t find myself bemoaning the Z5IIC’s performance, which is high praise indeed. And of course, the Nikon Z5IIC has an autofocus mod con that currently no other Nikon camera has – not even the flagship Nikon Z9 – and that’s fish subject-detection. The Pet Portraits Scene Mode instantly switched the camera to Animal-Detection AF (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) Now, I initially found this quite the novelty, but in a world of ever-expanding AF algorithms, why not? I actually used to know a professional photographer who photographed fish for fish-keeping publications, and I’m sure he’d be very happy indeed with this development. It’s exciting news for underwater photographers, too, because put a camera with fish AF in an underwater housing and you’re golden. Speaking of gold, I did my due diligence and found myself a fitting subject to test out this new autofocus mode. Thomas is a rescued fairground goldfish who resides in a local art studio owned by incredibly talented wildlife artist Jacqueline Byrne ( @jacquelinebyrne.art ). Jackie kindly allowed me to use Thomas as a model and I was pleased to find that the camera not only detected the goldfish’s body, but also locked onto his eyes. It did struggle at times, but the conditions were challenging. Reflections and scratches on the tank glass, not to mention underwater foliage, and my need to shoot wide open in low light, all contributed. But fish AF works and isn’t quite the joke addition it may at first seem. Fish AF isn’t the novelty you might think (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) The Nikon Z5IIC’s form factor certainly lends itself to videography, and just like the Nikon Z5 II it boasts some decent specs. Arguably the biggest selling point is internal 4K 30p full-width RAW video. And while it’s nice to have, I always thought it was a little out of place on the Nikon Z5II, and I still think it’s a little out of place on the Nikon Z5IIC. A lot of pro videographers don’t shoot RAW video. After all, it fills up storage as a pastime, creates increased internal heat, and is power-hungry in the edit. That said, it’s nice to have as an option. Although, a word of warning: make sure you’re using a capable SD card. The Nikon Z5IIC will only record RAW video on a memory card that’s over 32GB. And if your memory card isn’t fast enough, it’ll stop recording before time. When it comes to overheating, ambient temperature and camera usage will always affect the outcome, but I shot 13 minutes of uninterrupted RAW footage in real-world testing without issue. The Nikon ZR is proof that Nikon knows how to build a camera that’s very hard to overheat, and while I cannot comment on long-term video usage due to my very short time with the camera, I don’t have any immediate concerns. I also shot some 4K video. As you’d expect, the autofocus performed well; just be aware that 4K 60p enforces a 1.5x (DX) crop. (Image credit: Future / Mike Harris) Another video boon is in-body image stabilization. It’s not surprising given that the Nikon Z5II also has it, but it was a crucial inclusion because the Z5IIC’s direct competitors also have IBIS. What they don’t have is 7.5 stops of stabilization, with the camera beating the Panasonic Lumix S9’s 6.5 stops and the Sony A7C II’s seven stops. This is a great feature for photographers, too. I’d argue it’s essential for the Z5IIC given its viewfinderless design, because you’re not holding the camera up to your eye, which is the most stable shooting position. While the lower-resolution LCD screen didn’t really bother me when shooting stills, I do think it matters more for video. Metering is such an important part of videography, and while you’ve got aids such as zebras and histograms, every little helps if you’re not resorting to an external monitor. One thing I would suggest that any Nikon Z5IIC owner does is head into Menu>Setup>Monitor Brightness and set the latter to its maximum setting. This will reduce battery efficiency, but you’ll get a brighter and more visible screen. As a photographer, I lament the flip-out screen craze, much preferring a tilting screen, but the Nikon Z5IIC is a camera built to adapt to both worlds, and a flip-out screen is definitely preferable for video. with its 24.2-MP sensor. The bigger surprise is the Nikon Z5IIC’s performance in relation to the Nikon Z5 II, exhibiting sharper images between ISO3200 and ISO12,800. However, this could simply be a variation in optics, and in a real-world scenario, the difference is going to be negligible. Dynamic Range: Each camera boasts impressive dynamic range and despite differences in resolution, there really isn’t much to separate them. The Sony A7C II just about wins, as to be expected, but the Nikon Z5IIC more than holds its own, performing better than both the Nikon Z5 II and Panasonic Lumix S9. Again, the race is so tight, you’re unlikely to notice much difference in a real-world scenario. Signal to noise ratio: The lower-resolution sensors come out on top here, with the Sony A7C II’s higher resolution proving its undoing, although it doesn’t lag far behind. When it comes to the two Nikons and the Panasonic Lumix S9, you’d have to defer to a photo finish to work out who’s pipped who to the post, but it does look like the Nikon Z5IIC has outperformed the Nikon Z5 II once again. Nikon Z5IIC: Verdict The Nikon Z5IIC is a tale of two halves. On the one hand, it has a slightly awkward design. On the other, its performance punches above its weight. I’m no stickler for always looking through the viewfinder, but the biggest benefit of viewfinderless cameras is their increased portability. And yet, losing the viewfinder doesn’t impact the size and weight of the Z5IIC enough; it’s still a big lump. The upside of this is that it’s built like a tank and feels like a premium, weather-sealed product. I’m not saying the heft is a dealbreaker; just make sure you try it on for size before you buy. Under the hood is where the camera really gains some ground. It’s a fantastic all-around performer, with great autofocus, gorgeous stills, solid video specs, and impressive in-body image stabilization. Plus, you get the rather unusual (if superfluous) bonus of RAW video. Scene Modes is an unlikely standout for me. It really lives up to the Z5IIC’s ‘casual’ moniker and allows anybody to get creative with the camera from the offset. Picture Modes and Film Grain serve as the next step in creative agency, allowing you to apply ready-made or custom presets to your images in real time. Finally, the Nikon Z5IIC is competitively priced. At $1399.95 / £1,349, it sits between the Sony A7C II and Panasonic Lumix S9. It’s not a cheap camera by any means, and I do wonder how appealing that price point is to its ‘casual’ target audience. But it’s got the specs of a more expensive camera. Overall, I was ready to hate on the Nikon Z5IIC when it was announced, but I’ve been pleasantly surprised by how much I’ve enjoyed my limited time with the camera. That said, I wonder if its size and weight could be its undoing. It’s too big to be an everyday carry, and I fear it may be too intimidating for its ‘casual’ target audience. I hope I’m proved wrong, because this is a well-built, exceedingly capable full-frame camera. Just like its blueprint, the Nikon Z5 II. Design ★★★☆☆ I’m not sold on a viewfinderless design for a camera that’s this big and heavy, and the low-res LCD and lack of a joystick are disappointing. But it’s weather-sealed, very solidly built and comes with a nice deep grip. Photo Performance ★★★★☆ Gorgeous Nikon RAW files and accurate AF. The inclusion of Scene Modes makes it more accessible for newcomers, while Picture Controls and Film Grain are great ways to personalize images in-camera. Video Performance ★★★★☆ No open gate, but internal RAW video is impressive (if a little unnecessary). IBIS, 4K 60p (albeit cropped), reliable AF, a flip-out rear screen, and a riggable form factor are all solid video features. Value ★★★★☆ Sits between its closest rivals and will likely soon become the cheapest full-frame camera in Nikon’s mirrorless lineup. It’s not a cheap camera, but it’s competitively priced. Overall ★★★★☆ Nikon Z5IIC: Alternatives This little full-frame mirrorless camera arguably embodies the viewfinderless ethos better than the Nikon Z5IIC in that it’s noticeably smaller and lighter. The Panasonic Lumix S9 won’t beat the Nikon when it comes to stills, but it does boast some seriously good video specs, maxing out at 6K 30p open gate . The Sony A7C II is a few years old, but still a popular choice for those looking for a capable mirrorless camera with a more compact form factor. This camera’s genius is that it manages to squeeze in a rangefinder-style EVF. You also get a 33-MP sensor, but it does occupy a higher price bracket than either the Nikon Z5IIC or Panasonic Lumix S9. items.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 and iMac M6 Announced – 2nm Chip, ProRes RAW Media Engine, Up to 32GB Memory
items.summary_what: Apple MacBook Pro M6 and iMac M6 Announced – 2nm Chip, ProRes RAW Media Engine, Up to 32GB Memory: Apple has brought its 2nm M6 chip to the 14-inch MacBook Pro and the 24-inch iMac.

items.raw_content: Apple has brought its 2nm M6 chip to the 14-inch MacBook Pro and the 24-inch iMac. Both machines get two more CPU and GPU cores than before, Neural Accelerators in every GPU core, Wi-Fi 7 and a Media Engine with hardware ProRes and ProRes RAW support. For editors, the more important details sit further down the spec sheet: memory stops at 32GB, and the ports stay at Thunderbolt 4. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $1,999 and the iMac with M6 at $1,499. Pre-orders open tomorrow, October 28, and deliveries start on Friday, November 6. Both use the M6 chip that debuted in the Mac mini in August, which we covered in our Mac Studio and Mac mini launch article . In its full version, the M6 has a 12-core CPU (2 super cores, 4 performance cores and 6 efficiency cores), a 12-core GPU with a Neural Accelerator in each core, third-generation ray tracing, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine and up to 170GB/s of memory bandwidth. Unified memory starts at 16GB and goes up to 32GB. The Media Engine has one video decode engine, one video encode engine, one ProRes encode and decode engine and AV1 decode, with hardware acceleration for H.264, HEVC, ProRes and ProRes RAW. The entry-level iMac uses a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU version of the chip. Apple just released the new MacBook Pro 14-inch and iMac with its new M6 chip. Image credit: Apple The M6 chip and video work Apple’s performance claims for the MacBook Pro compare it with the 14-inch M5 model: up to 30 percent faster graphics, up to 25 percent faster AI workloads such as LLM prompt processing, and a Neural Engine that is up to 1.9x faster. The application examples in the press release are Blender ray tracing (up to 1.3x faster than M5), Affinity image processing (up to 1.2x) and Xcode builds (up to 1.3x). For the iMac, Apple compares against the M4 generation and quotes up to 2x faster graphics and up to 5x faster on-device AI prompt processing in LM Studio. Apple also claims the M6 has the world’s fastest CPU core. None of the figures Apple published for these two machines involves a video editing or grading application, so for filmmakers the Media Engine and memory configuration say more than the percentages. The Media Engine layout is the same as in the M5 Pro: one encoder, one decoder and one ProRes engine. The M5 Max doubles the encode and ProRes blocks. In practice, the M6 machines get hardware decoding for the formats most cameras record (H.264, HEVC, ProRes and ProRes RAW), but parallel exports, for example deliverables and proxies at the same time, share a single encoder. Formats outside that list, such as BRAW, R3D or ARRIRAW, rely on the CPU and GPU instead. After Effects on the new MacBook Pro 14-inch. Image credit: Apple Memory is the more obvious ceiling. Both machines top out at 32GB, and on the MacBook Pro the 16GB base configuration runs at 153GB/s; the full 170GB/s needs 24GB or 32GB. For 4K timelines in Final Cut Pro, Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve, 32GB is workable. Heavy noise reduction, Fusion compositions or 8K material are where the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro (up to 64GB at 307GB/s) or M5 Max becomes the more realistic option. We covered those models in our MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max launch article . MacBook Pro M6: XDR display, Thunderbolt 4 The 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display carries over: 3024 x 1964 pixels at 254ppi, up to 1,000 nits sustained full-screen, 1,600 nits peak for HDR content, a 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio, P3 wide color and ProMotion up to 120Hz. For editors, the fixed refresh rates of 47.95, 48, 50, 59.94 and 60Hz match playback to the project frame rate, and the reference modes include HDR Video (P3-ST 2084). A nano-texture version of the display is optional. Apple MacBook M6 14-inch, port situation. Image credit: Apple On the ports side, the M6 model has three Thunderbolt 4 ports at up to 40Gb/s, plus HDMI, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe 3 and a headphone jack. The M5 Pro and M5 Max models have three Thunderbolt 5 ports at up to 120Gb/s instead. The M6 drives up to two external displays at 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz, or one display at 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz. Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 are new. Apple rates the 72.4Wh battery at up to 24 hours of video streaming and up to 16 hours of wireless web use, and says performance is the same on battery and on mains power. The laptop ships with a 70W USB-C adapter; with a 96W or higher adapter, it charges to 50 percent in 30 minutes. It measures 31.26 x 22.12 x 1.55cm / 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61in and weighs 1.55kg / 3.4lb. Storage options are 1TB, 2TB or 4TB, and the colors are space black and silver. iMac M6: two models, two different port layouts The iMac comes in two versions, and the differences matter more for media work than the two extra cores suggest. The 10-core model has two Thunderbolt/USB 4 ports, supports one external display (up to 6K/60Hz), takes up to 24GB of memory and up to 1TB of storage, and has 2.5Gb Ethernet only as an option. The 12-core model has four Thunderbolt 4 ports, 2.5Gb Ethernet as standard, up to 32GB of memory, up to 2TB of storage, support for two external 6K displays (or one 8K/60Hz display) and an optional nano-texture glass. Both start with 16GB of memory and a 256GB SSD, which Apple says is up to 2x faster than in the M4 iMac. With 256GB, media has to live on external storage from day one. The iMac comes in whopping 7 color options. Still no return of the 27 inch version in sight, though. Image credit: Apple The 24-inch (23.5-inch viewable) 4.5K Retina display has a resolution of 4480 x 2520 pixels at 218ppi, 500 nits of brightness and P3 wide color with support for 1 billion colors. It has no XDR or HDR mode and no ProMotion, so the iMac is an SDR editing screen. The iMac also has a 12MP Center Stage camera, a six-speaker system with Spatial Audio and Dolby Atmos support, and a three-mic array. It comes in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver, measures 54.7 x 46.1cm / 21.5 x 18.1in and weighs 4.42kg / 9.7lb (10-core) or 4.44kg / 9.8lb (12-core). The new iMac M6 in use. Image credit: Apple Both ship with macOS 27 Both computers ship with macOS 27 Golden Gate, which includes Siri AI and new Apple Intelligence features. For edit systems, the more relevant point is software support. In our macOS 27 article for video editors , Adobe and Apple had confirmed support, while Blackmagic Design and Avid had not listed macOS 27 as qualified. New Macs generally cannot run a macOS version older than the one they ship with, so anyone buying one of these machines for client work should check their NLE, plugins and I/O drivers first. Where they fit The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is the entry point to Apple’s pro laptop line. It suits editors and shooters who cut 4K H.264, HEVC or ProRes, offload cards on location with the SDXC slot, and want an XDR display for HDR review away from the suite. Projects that need more than 32GB of memory, fast Thunderbolt 5 RAIDs or three external displays point to the M5 Pro version. The iMac is an all-in-one for SDR work: proxy editing, assistant editor stations, social and YouTube production, and offices that need a clean setup. For that work, the 12-core model is the better fit, as it adds the two extra Thunderbolt ports, the second external display and Ethernet as standard. Price and availability The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $1,999 ($1,899 for education) with 16GB of memory and a 1TB SSD. In Germany, Apple lists it from €2,299 including VAT. The iMac with M6 starts at $1,499 for the 10-core model and $1,699 for the 12-core model ($1,449 and $1,599 for education), and at €1,799 and €1,999 including VAT in Germany. Pre-orders open on October 28 in 35 countries and regions, and deliveries and in-store availability start on November 6. B&H and CVP do not list the new models yet. More details are in Apple’s announcements for the MacBook Pro and the iMac , and on the MacBook Pro and iMac tech specs pages. Would an M6 MacBook Pro or iMac cover your editing work, or do 32GB and Thunderbolt 4 push you to the M5 Pro? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below !

items.title: Feiyu Pocket 4 Announced – 1/1.55-Inch Sensor, 4K60, 111GB Built-In Storage
items.summary_what: Feiyu Pocket 4 Announced – 1/1.55-Inch Sensor, 4K60, 111GB Built-In Storage: FeiyuTech has launched the Feiyu Pocket 4, its new three-axis gimbal camera and the first update to the line since the Pocket 3.

items.raw_content: FeiyuTech has launched the Feiyu Pocket 4, its new three-axis gimbal camera and the first update to the line since the Pocket 3. The camera gets a much larger sensor than its predecessor, a 2.64-inch touchscreen that slides down to start shooting and up to cover the lens, and 111GB of internal storage. At $299, it costs a lot less than DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4, but the spec sheet also shows where the money was saved. The Feiyu Pocket 4 uses a 1/1.55-inch CMOS sensor with 50 megapixels behind a fixed-focus 110° lens at f/2.2. It records UHD 4K up to 60fps, 2.7K up to 60fps, and 1080p up to 120fps as H.264 or HEVC in an MP4 container, with a maximum bitrate of 80 Mbps. Stills go up to 8192 x 6144 pixels. A three-axis mechanical gimbal with up to 450° of pan travel stabilizes the image, and AI face and subject tracking work together with gesture control. The camera has 128GB of eMMC storage (about 111GB available to the user) and no microSD slot, and it weighs about 205g / 7.2oz. FeiyuTech sells the camera directly for $299, or $379 in a Creator Kit. We last covered FeiyuTech’s pocket cameras when the company introduced the Pocket 2 and Pocket 2S in 2021. Since then, this category has changed a lot. DJI released the Osmo Pocket 4 in April and the dual-lens Osmo Pocket 4P in July, and pocket gimbal cameras are now a major part of the market. Our analysis of how DJI and Insta360 now ship more cameras than the mirrorless industry gives the context. The Pocket 4 is FeiyuTech’s attempt to compete in this segment on price. Credit: FeiyuTech A sliding screen in place of a lens cap The most unusual part of the Pocket 4 is its mechanical design. The 2.64-inch touchscreen (480 x 480 pixels) sits on a sliding frame. Slide it down, and the camera powers on and is ready to shoot. According to FeiyuTech’s launch blog post , magnetic sensing detects the movement. Slide it up one step, and the gimbal motors lock. A second step extends a wraparound cover that encloses the camera head, so no separate case or clamp is necessary for transport. The square screen is also how FeiyuTech handles framing. The camera natively shoots 4:3, and the user can select 16:9 or vertical 9:16 on the touchscreen without physically turning the camera. According to the manual, vertical video goes up to 3K. The user can also rotate the camera 90° to enter the vertical mode. The body is made of aluminum-magnesium alloy and plastic, and it measures 140.5 x 52 x 31.7mm / 5.53 x 2.05 x 1.25in when folded. The Pocket 4 is not waterproof. Credit: FeiyuTech Sensor, lens and recording formats On paper, the 1/1.55-inch sensor is a large improvement over the Feiyu Pocket 3, which has a 1/2.3-inch, 12-megapixel sensor. It is still smaller than the 1-inch sensor in DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4. The 110° lens is wide for a vlogging camera, and the specifications list it as fixed focus. FeiyuTech’s FAQ states plainly that the Pocket 4 does not support autofocus. Thus, close-up product shots or face-to-camera recording at arm’s length can depend on the depth of field of the small sensor, not on a focus system. Video options include 4K at 24, 25, 30, 48, 50, and 60fps, 2.7K (2720 x 1520) at the same frame rates, and 1080p at up to 120fps. A separate slow-motion mode records at 2x or 4x in HD or Full HD. Time-lapse (static, dynamic, and motion), panorama, and a night mode are also available. ISO goes from 100 to 3200, and the electronic shutter goes from 16 seconds to 1/8000s. Users can switch between auto and manual exposure, select average or spot metering, and set flicker reduction to 50Hz or 60Hz. FeiyuTech does not list a log profile, a 10-bit mode, or an HDR mode on the product page or in the manual. The camera menu has a color option, but the company does not say what it includes. Photos are saved as JPG, and the product page also lists JPG+DNG. The maximum video bitrate of 80 Mbps is less than half of the 180 Mbps that DJI specifies for the Osmo Pocket 4. Tracking, gestures and gimbal control The mechanical ranges of the three-axis gimbal are −100° to +350° on pan, −185° to +134.5° on tilt, and −90° to +229.5° on roll, with a maximum controllable speed of 180° per second. The follow modes are: all follow, pan and tilt follow, and pan follow, and users can set the pan speed to slow, default, or quick. A five-way joystick controls the pan and tilt axes, and a double-tap switches it to digital zoom. Face tracking and subject tracking run on the camera itself; the user taps the subject on the touchscreen to select it. On the Pocket 3, tracking required the Feiyu Cam app. Gesture control has four commands: an OK sign starts or stops tracking, an open palm takes a photo or starts recording, a double L shape sets a custom composition, and a double thumbs-up switches gesture control off. The Feiyu Cam app ( iOS 13 or later, Android 6.0 or later) connects over 5GHz Wi-Fi and gives remote control, live preview, file transfer, and gimbal control through the phone’s motion sensors. Credit: FeiyuTech Storage, battery and connectivity The 111GB of user storage replaces the memory card completely. FeiyuTech says this holds approximately 875 minutes of Full HD video. At the maximum bitrate of 80 Mbps, the same storage holds roughly three hours of 4K footage. Users who shoot a full day of 4K must offload during the day. Files transfer over USB-C to a computer, directly to some phones over USB-C, or over Wi-Fi to the app. The Pocket 4 also works as a UVC webcam over USB-C. Power comes from an internal 1300mAh, 7.4V lithium-ion battery. FeiyuTech gives recording times of up to 2.5 hours at 1080p30, 1.8 hours at 4K30, and 1.5 hours at 4K60, measured at 25°C. Audio comes from the built-in microphone as 48kHz AAC. In FeiyuTech’s comparison table, it lists an external microphone as not supported for the Pocket 4, while the Pocket 3 supports one with a dedicated adapter. The Creator Kit includes a “Microphone & Battery Handle”, but FeiyuTech has not yet published specifications for this accessory. The camera also has a 1/4-inch thread on the base. How it compares with the DJI Osmo Pocket 4 The DJI Osmo Pocket 4 has a 1-inch sensor, 4K at up to 240fps, 10-bit D-Log ( a later firmware update extended it to slow motion), autofocus, 107GB internal storage plus a microSD slot, direct DJI Mic pairing, and timecode. It weighs 190.5g. In Europe, it started at €479 at launch. The Feiyu Pocket 4 is heavier and has no log profile, autofocus, external audio input, or card slot. Its advantages are the larger screen, the integrated lens cover, the larger internal storage, and the lower price. For readers who use a pocket gimbal camera as a B-camera in a professional production, the missing log profile and fixed focus are the main limitations. For travel and vlogging users who shoot mostly 8-bit footage for social media, the Feiyu Pocket 4 is a less expensive choice. Price and availability The Feiyu Pocket 4 is available now from the FeiyuTech online store . The Standard Kit costs $299 and includes the camera, a carrying bag, a USB-C to USB-C cable, a USB-A to USB-C adapter, a wrist strap, and the manual. The Creator Kit costs $379 and adds the Microphone & Battery Handle and a tripod. A portable bag ($49) and an adjustable extension pole ($39) are available separately. FeiyuTech ships from local warehouses in the US, Canada, the UK, and Germany, with free shipping to these regions. At the time of writing, B&H does not list the Pocket 4, and FeiyuTech has not published a euro price. items.raw_content: In his new book The Mineral Age, Tom Hagen takes aerial photographs of the mineral mines essential to our transition to low-carbon living. Everyone knows about the climate crisis. It's almost impossible to go a day without the news reporting on record-breaking phenomena; or, if you're unlucky, you'll experience the consequences first-hand. We all know we need to do our bit to live more sustainably, whether that's by recycling or using public transport. However, most people may be unaware of the resources enabling the world to transition to a more environmentally friendly lifestyle. These minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel, and copper, are part of a new frontier in humanity's quest to move away from fossil fuels. Because these rare earth elements are required for electric vehicles, batteries, and renewable energy infrastructure, demand is high. Photographer Tom Hegen's latest project, The Mineral Age, explores where these critical minerals come from and the environmental, social, and political consequences of extracting them. Compiled over the past six years, his book reveals the often-overlooked physical footprint of technological progress. Tom's interest in these landscapes began while photographing Germany's vast open-pit coal mines. Through this work, he became increasingly interested in humanity's quest to decarbonise its economies. "As I researched the energy transition more deeply, I realised that moving away from fossil fuels does not mean moving away from resource extraction," he explains. "Instead, we are entering a new era of mineral dependency. Many of these resources are concentrated in just a handful of countries, creating new geopolitical dependencies and vulnerabilities" While these minerals may ultimately lead to cleaner living, Tom reveals that their extraction often comes with significant environmental and social consequences which receive relatively little public attention. "This realisation became the starting point for The Mineral Age." Tom's most striking insight when putting the project together was the geographical imbalance between the consumption of these critical minerals and the impacts of their extraction. "Industrialised countries in the Global North are major consumers of minerals that are often extracted in developing regions of the Global South," he says. "This imbalance is shaped by geology, economic structures, cheaper labour, and weaker environmental regulations." He adds: "In some mining regions, environmental protections are poorly enforced, working conditions are hazardous, and local communities face serious consequences from industrial expansion. Child labour and human rights abuses also remain significant concerns in certain mining sectors." It became increasingly clear to Tom that the environmental and social costs of technological progress are often shouldered by communities which are far removed from those who ultimately benefit from it. "We tend to celebrate the promise of clean technologies without paying much attention to the landscapes being transformed to make them possible," he says. "In many ways, we are shifting part of the environmental burden of our consumption to other regions of the world, keeping the consequences largely out of sight." This isn't to say The Mineral Age argues against the shift away from fossil fuels, though. "Rather, I believe we need to acknowledge that even technologies designed to create a more sustainable future have a substantial material footprint." Tom's photographic practice is strongly research-driven, and The Mineral Age is no exception. Before travelling, he spends considerable time investigating global mineral supply chains, identifying significant mining regions, and studying the industrial processes involved. "Accessing these places is often one of the greatest challenges," he says. "Many mining operations are extremely remote, heavily restricted, or kept out of public view. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, it took me more than two years to arrange access to some of the mining sites. Every photograph in The Mineral Age was taken from an elevated perspective. Tom primarily works with heavy-lift drones carrying a high-resolution medium-format camera. "When drone operations are not possible, I photograph from helicopters or small aircraft. The aerial perspective allows me to reveal the immense scale of these industrial landscapes." The Mineral Age will contain 247 aerial photographs, which Tom believes will spark curiosity, encourage conversations, and make the complex topic of energy transition more accessible. "My intention is not to provide simple answers, but to raise awareness of the often-invisible consequences of our demand for resources," he says. "Ultimately, The Mineral Age is about the landscapes behind our modern lives, and the consequences of building the future."

items.raw_content: What happens when a horror thriller borrows the visual language of a western? A feature like Dark Sky Films’ Cruel Hands is born. The synopsis for the film reads: Amid the worst bushfires in Australia’s history, Maria (Mavournee Hazel) and her son Dai (Diesel La Torraca) escape a violent and abusive husband and make their way to an abandoned farmhouse. While hiding, Maria tries to create a new home for Dai as Jason (Josh McConville), the police, and the fires close in. In a climactic battle, two damaged, traumatized parents fight over Dai's fate, with deadly consequences. For Cruel Hands , DP Charlie Cole used bold compositions, locked-off frames, and deliberate dolly movements to give the film a Western-inspired aesthetic, heightening the tension as a man hunts down his estranged wife and child. The result is a striking visual contrast between the film’s suspenseful pursuit and the more intimate, emotionally grounded moments at its center. In the interview below, Cole breaks down the cinematography behind Cruel Hands and discusses his collaboration with longtime friend and director Al Kalyk. Cruel Hands is available to rent or buy on Prime Video . It is also available on Plex . - YouTube www.youtube.com No Film School: How did you first discover your passion for cinematography? Was there a particular film whose visual style or cinematography made you realize this was the path you wanted to pursue? Charlie Cole: I fell in love with cinematography through a handful of films that I saw within a year. At the time, I was a Drawing major at Pratt Institute, and my roommate and I watched Enter the Void and Antichrist . A few months later, I watched Requiem For A Dream - those 3 films together shook me out of wanting to be a fine artist, and pulled me into the life of filmmaking. All of them shared a similar approach to me: If you have a challenging (hard to watch) script, shoot it beautifully - this will make the audience engage with the poetry of the visuals and open their hearts more to what the film is saying. If people are prepared for a jump scare, they are guarded. These three films impacted me so deeply, and I think a large part of that is due to the cinematography being quite poetic in each case. I watched them unguarded, and therefore the films affected me deeply. NFS: How did you become involved with Cruel Hands and what did pre-production look like for you? CC: The director, Al Kalyk, and I attended the American Film Institute together and had worked on several projects. He has become one of my best friends, and it just felt right that I would shoot his first feature. We had been talking about it on and off for a few years before it got wings and financing. Pre-pro was 6 weeks in Australia. We shot the film in January. (Australian summer), so we did about a month of solid prep on the Gold Coast (where the film was shot), then 2 weeks of Al and me prepping over Christmas and New Year's while in Sydney. It was a pretty magical experience. One I hope to get to experience again. DP Charlie Cole on 'Cruel Hands' Credit: ProjectionPR NFS: Can you talk about the collaboration between you and Cruel Hands director Al Kalyk? How did you align your artistic visions for this project? CC: Our collaboration was very friendly and trusting. Al and I are like brothers. My initial thoughts for the visuals on the film were far more brooding and muddy compared to where we landed. I had sent Al a fairly extensive lookbook, which served as my initial take on the script before seeing any of his ref images. Immediately, Al let me know I was wrong (in a loving way). He had this wonderful idea to shoot this film in part like an old western film. Ultimately, the film lends itself to both styles, I feel: There’s a duality between bold-angled, western locked-off or dolly shots when we’re in the thriller parts of the film where Jason is hunting down his ‘escaped’ wife and child, and a more delicate sensibility when we are sitting with Dai and Maria, a mother and son trying to emotionally survive this new chapter in their lives and hopefully get closer along the way. Visually, Al and I are quite in tune stylistically. We’ve never really had issues syncing up with how we both feel about images. Al brings a lot of paintings as references, while I bring a lot of cinematic references. During prep, I put together a Visual Bible of the film, which is every scene broken down into Tone, Lighting, and Framing. I make sure that Al approves of every image, and it’s built very much based on our conversations about the film and how the visuals push the story forward. After about a month or so of putting that document together, the film’s visual language is very fine-tuned. Now it’s just a matter of making it. NFS: Walk us through your camera, lens, and filtration choices, and how they supported the tone of Cruel Hands ? CC: Right off the bat, my instinct was to shoot this film in Large Format. We were going to be dealing with small rural spaces that we wanted to feel Cinematic. LF was our choice to capture that, but we were naturally concerned with the lens choices available, especially since we were locked into a rental house in rural Australia that our Producer had set up an excellent bargain with. Luckily for us, the rental house (Cine 2481) had everything we needed! After 2 days of testing, we ended up selecting the following combination: CAM: Mini LF (4.5k Open Gate) LENSES: Leica R FILTRATION: Low Con // Black Satin One of our main references for the look of the film was Phantom Thread . We wanted to create a softness and delicacy in the lenses that counteracted the boldness of the western style (dolly push-ins / tense angles, dark lighting). I’m very happy with where we ended up. NFS: Looking back on Cruel Hands , is there a creative or technical achievement you are especially proud of that viewers may not realize while watching the finished film? CC: The film takes place during the wildfires of 2019, so we knew we would have to build that look into the world. The air gets choked with smoke, and all the light turns a deep orange. So, in the third act of the film, when the fires have started (further away from our character, but slowly impeding), we build the intensity of smoke and color. To achieve this, we had to instill a strict ‘no direct sun’ rule for shooting any scene that took place in the third act. This meant only shooting exteriors at dusk, dawn, or overcast moments (rare in Australia’s summer). Then we had an amazing, helpful team of art department / PA’s / grips who would help control the 2 household hazers and 1 fogger; we had to spread out the smoke as best we could. I’m really happy with the effect of feeling like you’re surrounded by wildfires. So much of what you see in the film is all practical. Color (done by Al Kalyk), of course, helps a ton with the feeling of burnt skies, along with additional smoke effects added in post by our VFX team for the final scenes. 'Cruel Hands' BTS Credit: ProjectionPR NFS: You also had a film, Corpus , recently premiering at the Fantasia International Film Festival. Can you tell us about the look of that film? CC: Oof, that is a fun film. The film takes place in the early 2000s NYC and is an erotic body horror thriller. The film is a mix of the NYC club scene, dingy apartments, and a remote mansion in upstate NYC. The look of the film ranges within those worlds; director Corrin Evans and I maintained deep colors and sensual tones. The film is meant to feel hot and sweaty, full of shadows. It is for sure a summer movie- we shot on the Super Baltars for a rich, warm, human feeling. Production Designer Sadra Tehrani brought so much of this world to life, and we collaborated in incorporating so much of the lighting into practicals. The whole film is shot with Tungsten and HMI lighting for a heavier, more period-honest look. The majority of the shots and setups were oner-focused, letting the handheld camera roam around the characters, with little to no marks and a guided sense of where we needed the emotions to come out in the scenes. The actors were amazing, very game for all of it, extremely consistent and dedicated. Focus Puller / 1st AC Julia Crytser made so many of the moves possible. We were almost always shooting wide open on a 100mm with no marks, just flowing. Corpus also just won Best Cinematography at Brooklyn Horror Fest! I just found out this morning, as I’m writing this. NFS: Both Cruel Hands and Corpus fall into the horror genre. Why do you think you've found such a strong creative home in the genre, and what keeps you returning to it? CC: I love the horror genre! I like when it’s mixed in with other genres. Horror - thriller /drama/romance. Horror tends to bring a tension in the tension. There is inevitably some duality, deceit, mystery, and intrigue. All of these lend themselves to interesting images and approaches. In horror, you can go so many visual routes. It can be clean and disturbing ( Backroom, Midsommar, The Substance ) or gritty and dark ( Blair Witch ). Underneath it all, with both Cruel Hands and Corpus , it’s a story of longing for those you love, and how you’ll do anything to be closer to them. NFS: What sequence in both Corpus and Cruel Hands required the most planning, and how did you and your team execute it? Cruel Hands has a big, fiery, violent climax (sorry, spoiler!) That was a difficult sequence to pull off; we had a large wide, stunts, weapons, fire, smoke, and of course it took place at dusk. We also needed a very specific terrain (a clearing within a forest) and a fallen tree that one of the characters hides behind (this tree ended up being dragged in through the forest on a forklift - Australians will get the job done, let me tell ya). We pulled this off with elaborate planning and several scouts. The fire effect was kind of simple when you break it down. Large sources far away, and hidden behind tree lines, hills, bushes. Then blast them with smoke so we get a huge backlight. The smoke helped us light because it carries the light everywhere. Supplement with a few lights and voila — fiery climax smoke battle! Corpus had a few challenging scenes. The climax is (surprise surprise) also violent. This scene has a bunch of stunts and prosthetics involved, and took 2.5 days to shoot. The scene is in a large room with tons of windows. Of course, the first day was sunny, the second was raining, and the third was partially cloudy. The lighting continuity credit goes to Gaffer Claire Halloran and Sophia Williams, who kept us on track and kept the look consistent while we shot in nearly every direction over those days. I would be remiss not to mention the large opening scene of Corpus that takes place in a huge club called Red Light Dharma. We had about 200 extras and had to light a massive warehouse. No particular trick to it, except that we knew we needed to have 360-degree visibility in the scene, so PD Sadra Tehrani and I worked to make all the lights we needed practical. The teams pulled it off so well - we were able to see everything in the frame, and only used lights that would have existed at the time, and in those venues, for more authenticity. Corrin Evans (director) was so good about fighting for that throughout the film. 'Cruel Hands' Credit: ProjectionPR NFS: How would you describe your visual style, and how do you adapt it across films like Cruel Hands and Corpus ? My visual style lies in intimacy and intrigue. I love a curious camera. My background is in fine arts; I went to school for drawing. And a lesson that always stuck with me was when a professor reminded us all - everyone here knows how to draw - what makes your drawing special. I try to keep that lesson alive with cinematography. Another drawing professor (that school clearly had a big impact on me ;) - thank you, Pratt Institute!) said that when you bring a piece up to show to the class, you should feel nervous. You should feel vulnerable. As a cinematographer, we are so protected by the camera; we risk nothing. The actors and directors are analyzed/criticized. I try to use that safe privilege to try and show as much of what I’m feeling as possible. And hopefully it comes across in the images.

items.raw_content: The London studio began rebranding the psychic services platform with a chakra reading and a little charcoal, and the result is a rich, purple-hued brand world that feels alive. It's almost Halloween, so forgive me if, on discovering that a branding project began with a séance, I immediately thought of that brilliant 'Day-O' dinner party scene in Beetlejuice. You know, the one with the late great Catherine O'Hara? I presume no one at Mother Design was forced into an impromptu calypso number, but it's a wonderful mental image. What actually happened involved way less dancing and uncontrolled lip syncing. The independent design studio, part of the Mother Family, has crafted a new identity for Purple Garden, the mobile and online psychic services platform. Fittingly, the team decided to lean into a more spiritual approach to get there. The brief was to "bring the feeling of spiritual practice into the digital world", which was no easy task. The spiritual services industry is worth around $2.3 billion, and apps and online platforms are opening up new ways for people to connect with guidance. But things can get lost in translation on screen: the atmosphere, ritual, and energy – it's hard to replicate online when you're not in the room. Mother Design's job was to fix that. The new brand therefore reframes Purple Garden from somewhere you visit for a one-off reading into a home for ongoing spiritual practice. It's built on a rather lovely insight: some questions keep returning no matter how much life changes. The audience, which Mother calls 'Believers of the Bigger Picture', are "seasoned seekers" looking for growth and meaning. So the creative idea, 'A Living Practice', moves from passive advice to active clarity through repetition and growth. How did Mother Design figure all this out? They staged a séance and a chakra reading, alongside an automatic drawing and writing workshop led by one of Purple Garden's holistic practitioners. It's what we've come to expect from the studio, as it encourages its team to experiment with unfamiliar disciplines. Armed with paper and charcoal, they worked instinctively, trying to ignore and bypass conscious thought. The forms and feelings that emerged from the session then became the foundation of the identity. "So much of spiritual practice is about things you feel rather than things you can see – energy, intuition, connection and those moments when you feel altered somehow," says Joanna Tulej, creative director at Mother Design. "The challenge was how you translate that into a brand experience without falling back on the visual clichés of the category. "We realised that if we wanted the identity to feel spontaneous and alive, we needed to allow some of that spontaneity into the way we designed it too. Starting with the séance and automatic drawing session gave us permission to step away from the screen and the rational design process. Some of the textures, energy and unexpectedness that came out of that experience found their way into the final identity." I absolutely love this. Whatever you make of spirituality, it's nice to remember that the best work comes from being experimental and having fun. I think we need that now more than ever. I was also fascinated to learn that the approach was partly inspired by the Swedish artist Hilma af Klint and The Five, the collective of brilliant women who experimented with trance-like states and automatic drawing to ignore conscious thought and let images and words emerge freely. (If you've not heard of her, look her up! Her paintings are considered to be among the first major abstract works in Western art history.) But the inventiveness didn't stop at charcoal. During development, Mother Design moved back and forth between traditional design software and AI tools, iterating constantly to generate unexpected visuals and add more unpredictability to the process. Looking at the outcome, I'll start with the typography because you can see all this play spilling through. The wordmark itself balances modern with whimsical. Elongated serifs and curved corners seem to grow outward. A "digital-first", crystal-like glyph acts as a symbol of guidance and forms the basis of the entire icon system for navigating the platform's many services. Literatura Present and ABC Social complete the type system. Literatura's flowing descenders and serifs add to that sense of growth, and ABC Social does the functional, sensible stuff so things are easy to read on screen. I really love the "living type" detail, inspired by cymatic patterns. That's the shape sound makes when it vibrates through a surface, if you didn't know. The subtle message is that Purple Garden helps you to grow, too. Colour-wise, purple clearly takes the lead. But Mother Design has developed a palette of six warmer purples, deliberately moving away from the cool, blue-toned purples so common in this category. The imagery feels more intimate and tactile, while the motion reinforces the idea of growth. The project follows Mother Design's recent rebrand of Keen , another spiritual guidance brand within the Ingenio portfolio. While Keen targeted a more mainstream, "spiritually curious" audience, Purple Garden is for those already seasoned in this space: two brands, two different jobs. "Purple Garden is for people who already have a deep connection with spirituality and see it as an active part of how they navigate their lives," says Ariana Hellebuyck, CMO at Ingenio. "We wanted the brand to reflect the depth of the experiences our guides provide and make that connection feel just as powerful in a digital environment. "Mother Design has created something that feels distinctive to Purple Garden and true to our audience, while giving us a richer and more immersive platform for the next stage of the brand." The new identity is now being rolled out across Purple Garden's website, app, advertising, and social channels over the coming weeks. It's got me thinking about how I love to switch off. Admittedly, my rituals are less mystical and don't involve any summoning. I find ironing, getting out on my bike, or spending time in the garden helps me zone out. Not as exciting, but the principle is the same. Just like Hilma, this project reminds us to play and try new things. Don't be afraid to experiment. And let creativity flow. You never know what will come out the other side.

items.raw_content: Sigma is a company that does things their way, I don't think they think all that much about what others are doing with lens design, and they definitely don't care what others are doing with cameras. They're a lot like Leica, but a lot more affordable. The Sigma BF is definitely its own thing, and the fp2 is too.. These are small companies in the grand scheme of things. It's better to be you than chasing the giants. It's working very well for both of them. Sigma fp2 Sigma has announced the FP2, the world's smallest full-frame camera. The camera measures 112.8 x 69.9 x 41.8 mm / 4.4 x 2.8 x 1.6 in and weighs in at 460g with the battery and card. In a full-frame camera, that's quite impressive. Canon's smallest camera is the EOS R50 V and measures 116 x 85.5 x 68.8 mm / 4.6 x 3.4 x 2.7 in and weighs 370g with the battery. So if you've had an R50 V in your hands, that'll give you an idea of the size. The big caveat being the APS-C sensor. The fp2 is almost a complete ground up re-design, a refresh it is not. They have added a 3.15″ tilt screen, and a bigger battery and it's even a bit smaller than its predecessor. The camera is somehow equipped with two USB-C ports and a full-size HDMI port. The fp2 is equipped with a partially stacked image sensor, which in turn should lead to faster readout speeds and less rolling shutter. We'll have to wait for the official numbers on that topic, but faster is usually better when it comes to sensors. If you want to shoot some action stuff, the 20fps is generally more than enough for most people. Another interesting feature is the 70GB of internal storage. I have a camera with internal storage and it's so annoying that I never use it. Hopefully Sigma has a better implementation. The camera is no slouch on the video side of things. 6K open gate video, with 12-bit ProRes RAW to SSD. Sigma claims 14.1 stops of dynamic range with L-raw in 4K. You also get dual base ISO settings and 32-bit float audio. That's pretty impressive. Some consider the FP2 a “modular” camera, as Sigma offers bevy of accessories to fit your needs. New Accessories As mentioned, Sigma is also launching a lot of accessories for the fp2. They aren't cheap, but that's probably because this will not be a mass market camera, and it comes down to economies of scale. Hopefully they're well made and do what they do well, especially the EVF and LCD Viewfinder. Sigma fp2 Accessories Sigma EVF-21 Electronic Viewfinder 5.76M-dot OLED with eye sensor.
