items.raw_content: Last week, a fisherman went viral after sharing dramatic footage of a fin whale bursting through the surface of the sea during a feeding frenzy off the coast of West Wales. Rhys Morgan, an oil refinery shift team leader and avid fisherman, was on a fishing excursion near the Celtic Deep, a 100m depression in the sea floor close to the Pembrokeshire coastline, when the whale appeared. “When they [whales] pop up near the boat, you really do feel small out there,” Morgan told The Guardian , after explaining that he “always” has his drone to hand when out fishing, having bought one in 2025. However, what Morgan didn’t share with The Guardian , nor in the Instagram post that included the incredible footage, was which drone he uses. We do know from a hashtag included in that Instagram post that he uses a DJI drone, but the exact model remains unknown. Watch: fishermen Rhys Morgan used a DJI drone to capture this fin whale feeding off the West Wales coast We do know that Rhys Morgan regularly uses a DJI Air 3S – a drone we recommend for its all-round flexibility – and this is the one we would use in this scenario. This drone balances optical power, stealth, and flight capabilities well, making it a good choice for filming wildlife like whales. The UK government says all marine wildlife watchers must stay at least 100m (330 feet) away from animals, and that drones shouldn’t be used if they’ll disturb an animal. The Air 3S features a 70mm medium telephoto lens with 3x optical zoom, which enables capturing tight, intimate footage of whale behaviors – such as breaching, tail slapping, or spyhopping – while keeping the drone positioned more than 100 meters away. What’s more, with 4K/60fps and 4K/100fps slow-motion recording, as long as the conditions aren’t too harsh, there’s no reason why you shouldn’t come away with crisp footage. Speaking of conditions, the DJI Air 3S has a Level 5 Beaufort scale rating – the Beaufort scale being a widely recognized international scale ranging from 0 to 12, used to estimate wind speed and its effects on land and sea. Level 5 means the DJI drone can handle wind speeds of around 19–24 mph (8.5-10.7 m/s), which is standard for most popular mid-to-high-end consumer camera drones. Of course, there are other solid alternatives for filming the kind of footage Morgan shot of the fin whale, and my other picks would probably be the Autel Robotics Evo Lite+ (for higher budgets) and the Potensic Atom (leaner budgets). If you want to dive deeper into your options, be sure to check out our in-house drone expert Adam Juniper’s pick of the best camera drones . You might also like… Not into drones but love wildlife? We’ve also got a roundup of the best cameras for wildlife photography !

items.title: Hollyland LARK M3 Explained – One Transmitter, Up to Four Receivers, and 4-Track Audio
items.summary_what: Hollyland LARK M3 Explained – One Transmitter, Up to Four Receivers, and 4-Track Audio: Most budget wireless kits are built around one assumption: one receiver, one camera.
items.summary_why: Contains hardware performance adjustments, autofocus enhancements, or sensor/codec improvements.
items.summary_action: Test new release on a backup or non-critical test project before upgrading active production timelines.
items.raw_content: Most budget wireless kits are built around one assumption: one receiver, one camera. The Hollyland LARK M3 breaks that assumption, because a single transmitter can feed up to four receivers at the same time. On a multi-camera interview, that means every camera can record the same clean lav signal instead of scratch audio. Here is how the system divides control between receivers, where the four isolated tracks actually arrive, and where its limits are. We have previously covered the LARK M2 and the more discreet LARK M2S , as well as the LARK MAX 2 , which adds onboard recording and timecode. The M3 sits between those approaches. It keeps the 9g (0.32oz) transmitter size of the M2 while adding 32-bit float output and much more flexible multi-transmitter and multi-receiver routing. The LARK M3 is a 2.4GHz system with a 9g (0.32oz) transmitter, 48kHz audio at 24-bit or 32-bit float, three levels of AI noise cancellation, and a rated range of up to 300m (1,000ft). It scales in both directions: one receiver accepts up to four transmitters, and one transmitter pairs with up to four receivers, in any combination up to 4TX and 4RX. Two receiver types are available: a 5.9g (0.21oz) USB-C receiver for phones, tablets, and computers, and a 20g (0.71oz) camera receiver with 3.5mm TRS output and a USB-C port. One lav, several cameras On a typical two-camera interview with a single wireless kit, the receiver goes on the A camera. The B camera records its onboard microphone as a reference, and the editor syncs the angles by waveform and uses the A-camera audio for the whole scene. The LARK M3 removes that step. A second, third, or fourth receiver pairs to the same transmitter, so each camera records the lav signal directly. The same applies to mixed setups, which Hollyland confirms in its FAQ: camera receivers and USB-C receivers can work together in one system as long as the total is four receivers or fewer. A presenter can feed a cinema camera, a phone recording a vertical version, and a laptop running a live stream from one transmitter. Transmitters and receivers can also be added or removed during a shoot without interrupting audio on the units that stay connected. Hollyland has followed a similar logic on the video side. The Pyro Ultra wireless video system supports an unlimited number of receivers, and the LARK M3 brings a smaller version of that one-to-many idea to entry-level audio. LARK M3 kit. Image credit: Hollyland How the primary and secondary receivers divide control When more than one receiver is connected, the system assigns roles automatically. According to the manual, the first receiver that connects after the transmitter powers on becomes the primary receiver, and every receiver after it becomes a secondary. The primary receiver controls the transmitters: noise cancellation, mute, the indicator lights, voice tuning presets, and Smart Reverb. Two settings stay independent on every receiver: output gain and channel mode. Each camera can therefore run its own level and channel configuration without changing the transmitter settings for the rest of the system. If the primary receiver goes offline during a take, the system selects one of the remaining receivers as the new primary while audio on the secondary receivers continues. The roles can be changed. In the app, a secondary receiver can be promoted to primary, or the crew can disconnect all receivers except the one that should take control, and then reconnect the others. Four independent tracks. Image credit: Hollyland Where the four isolated tracks actually arrive The headline feature of four independent tracks needs precise reading, because it depends on the connection. According to Hollyland’s manual and FAQ, the LARK M3 can record up to four isolated tracks, but only through compatible digital connections. The camera receiver’s 3.5mm TRS output is limited to Mono or Stereo, so four separate tracks require the separately sold LARK M3 Hot Shoe Adapter or a USB-C connection to a computer with compatible recording software. On phones, 4-Track mode depends on the app. Hollyland’s FAQ says compatible third-party recording apps on iOS can support it, while the native camera apps on iOS and Android do not. The same applies to 32-bit float: it requires compatible software, and Android devices are limited to 24-bit. Hollyland LARK M3 compact kit. Image credit: Hollyland Practical configurations The flexible transmitter and receiver arrangement is what makes the M3 different from a conventional two-person wireless kit. For a two-person interview on two cameras, both cameras can receive the same two microphones directly. For a four-person panel, four transmitters can feed one receiver, with four isolated tracks available through a compatible digital connection. A single presenter can instead feed several receivers at once, allowing the same microphone to reach a camera, phone and computer simultaneously. The system can therefore be built around either the number of people being recorded or the number of devices that need to receive the audio. Two transmitter, four receiver kit. Image credit: Hollyland Current limitations The LARK M3 transmitters do not have internal recording, and the system does not support timecode. A triple press of the transmitter button starts and stops recording on the connected device, not in the microphone. If the 2.4GHz link drops, no backup copy exists on the transmitter. Multiple receivers reduce some of that risk because each camera or device holds its own received copy of the audio, but all copies still depend on the same wireless transmission. Battery life is approximately eight hours per transmitter with noise cancellation off, and 4 to 4.5 hours with it on. The camera receiver runs for approximately nine hours, and receivers can run continuously on USB-C power. Hollyland rates the 300m (1,000ft) range for open environments without interference. How it compares within the LARK lineup The LARK M3 keeps the compact 9g (0.32oz) transmitter format of the LARK M2 while adding 32-bit float output, AI noise cancellation, support for up to four transmitters and four receivers, and four-track recording through compatible digital connections. The LARK MAX 2 moves further toward professional production. Its transmitters add onboard 32-bit float recording and timecode, giving crews a backup copy and a more complete sync workflow. The M3 therefore makes the most sense when the priority is a small microphone and flexible routing between several people, cameras, or recording devices. The MAX 2 remains the stronger option when internal backup recording and timecode are more important. Price and availability The LARK M3 is available now in four kits. The 2TX&1RX kit is priced at $99 , the 2TX&2RX kit is $119 , the 2TX&4RX kit is $179 , and the 4TX&2RX kit costs $179 . B&H also sells single components: a transmitter at $39, a USB-C receiver at $29, and a camera receiver at $39. The hot shoe adapter is sold separately. For more information, please visit the Hollyland website . Would one transmitter feeding several cameras change how you rig your next interview, or is backup recording a requirement before a kit goes on a multi-camera shoot? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

items.title: Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function
items.summary_what: Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function: In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment.

items.raw_content:
In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment. But when I heard that the native CSS random() function landed in Safari and is rolling out in Chrome 156, I started wondering: where does randomness actually make sense on the web? Is it something we want in our design system? To find out, I did what I always do in doubt: I built a bunch of playful CodePen demos exploring organic typography, bouncing letters, splayed cards, and a punk fanzine. As someone who loves building design systems and tinkering with CSS architecture, a big part of my day job revolves around control. We set up spacing scales, lock down typography, set up color tokens, and make sure everything aligns on a grid. Consistency is usually our bread and butter as design engineers and a proud badge of skill when creating design systems. If a card suddenly jumps 20 pixels to the left on a refresh, it’s not creative expression; it’s a bug that the project manager will log. So when I first heard that the native random() function from the CSS Values and Units Level 5 spec was shipped in Safari, and is currently rolling out in Chrome 156 (with positive signals from Mozilla on Firefox as well), my first reaction was: that’s pretty cool! And my second reaction was: wait... where would I actually use this without making a mess? How can I convince designers that random might be a good idea for a design system? Because let’s be honest: why on earth would we want randomness in our stylesheets when we’ve spent the last decade trying to make the web more predictable? Even when using flexbox or fluid typography, we’re still trying to make things as aligned and uniform as possible. The Charm Of Things Not Being 100% Straight If you step away from the browser for a second and look at physical things around you, nothing is ever truly uniform. Take an old letterpress print: the ink bleeds slightly into the paper grain, some letters have a microscopic tilt, and the baseline isn’t always that straight. Or think about a deck of Polaroid photos dropped on a coffee table; those photos aren’t perfect, probably not straight either. Or what about lights flickering in a street at night? That little bit of analog messiness is what makes things feel alive , organic , and human . On the web, we’ve gotten so good at pixel perfection that sometimes our interfaces end up feeling a bit sterile. We notice this even more now with rapidly created designs by an unguided LLM; we usually end up with the same sort of design we had 10 years ago. Everything is squared off, aligned, neat. It works, but frankly, it does get a bit boring. Randomness in CSS doesn’t have to mean throwing your design system out the window. It’s about little imperfections and playfulness. Maybe let’s even call it fun. To see what this actually looks like in practice, I spent a few hours tinkering in CodePen. The demos might feel a bit isolated, but I’m sure that many designers could make the best of this controlled chaos . But before we look at those demos, let’s take a look at the syntax. How The CSS random() Function Works The random() function is specified in CSS Values and Units Module Level 5 . It generates a pseudo-random value inside your CSS without needing JavaScript or a build-time Sass loop. The formal specification looks like this: random( ?, , , ? ) In practice, and across current browser implementations, you can just write comma-separated arguments: /* Random angle between -3deg and 3deg */ rotate: random(-3deg, 3deg); /* Random width between 20px and 80px in steps of 10px */ inline-size: random(20px, 80px, 10px); /* Random animation duration */ animation-duration: random(1.5s, 3s, 0.2s); Matching Units It won’t be a shocker for most people, but I thought I should at least mention that your minimum and maximum bounds must share the exact same unit type . The CSS parser needs to know what dimension it’s dealing with. You can use lengths, angles, time, percentages, or plain unitless numbers: /* Good: both are angles */ rotate: random(-4deg, 4deg); /* Good: both are unitless numbers */ opacity: random(0.3, 1); /* Nope! You cannot mix units */ inline-size: random(2rem, 100px); /* Invalid */ If you ever need to combine units, you’ll have to reach for calc() inside the arguments so each side resolves properly. Stepping And Rounding The optional third argument is the step size. If you don’t add it, the browser picks from a continuous range. But if you provide a step, it rounds the random value to discrete increments: /* Only produces 0px, 15px, 30px, 45px, or 60px */ top: random(0px, 60px, 15px); This can be helpful in cases where you want things to jump around a bit, but you still want them to land on your pre-defined grid. Caching Keys: Keeping Things In Sync Normally, every time random() is evaluated on a property, it creates an independent random value. But there could be an example where you create a box that sets inline-size and block-size at random, but at the same time you need them to match so the element stays a perfect square. That’s where the caching key comes in: .card-thumbnail { /* Both properties share the key --square-size */ inline-size: random(--square-size element-scoped, 60px, 120px); block-size: random(--square-size element-scoped, 60px, 120px); } In the latest spec, a bare dashed ident like --square-size shares its seed globally across every element in the document (which would make all cards identical). To keep width and height linked on a single element while giving each card its own independent size, the spec requires pairing it with the element-scoped keyword (e.g. --square-size element-scoped ). To see this in action, I created a little example. In the top row, the tiles have uncached dimensions, which distorts each tile into an unpredictable, mismatched rectangle. In the bottom row, both inline-size and block-size share --square-size , guaranteeing that each tile remains a pristine 1:1 square. Refresh the CodePen a couple of times and notice the bottom cards keeping the same randomness: See the Pen Uncached vs cached random() [forked] by @utilitybend . /* Uncached: width and height resolve independently, creating random rectangles */ .tile-uncached { inline-size: random(4.2rem, 8.5rem); block-size: random(4.2rem, 8.5rem); rotate: random(-3.5deg, 3.5deg); } /* Cached: shared key guarantees a clean 1:1 square */ .tile-cached { inline-size: random(--square-size element-scoped, 4.2rem, 8.5rem); block-size: random(--square-size element-scoped, 4.2rem, 8.5rem); rotate: random(--tilt element-scoped, -3.5deg, 3.5deg); } Browser Support And Progressive Enhancement Where can you test this today? WebKit / Safari : Safari was the first to land support. Chrome / Edge : Shipped and rolling out right now with Chrome 156 . Firefox : Positive signals on the standards track, so hopefully won’t be too far behind. Because we’re still in the rollout phase, you’ll want to wrap your experiments in @supports : /* Baseline for all browsers */ .badge { rotate: 0deg; } /* Enhanced for browsers with random() */ @supports (rotate: random(-2deg, 2deg)) { .badge { rotate: random(-2.5deg, 2.5deg); } } The Future random-item Function There’s also another function in the spec called random-item() . While random() handles numerical ranges, random-item() lets you pick from a list of predefined tokens or keywords: /* Picking a random color from your palette */ background-color: random-item(--seed, oklch(75% 0.18 150), oklch(65% 0.22 350), oklch(85% 0.16 85)); This can be handy to randomise from a set of design tokens. This one does not have any browser support at the moment, but it certainly is something to look forward to. And now for the practical part. Demo 1: Let’s Just Randomize Letters When I started playing with the feature, I was also doing some typography tricks with animations. So that’s where my first thought went: Typography! What if we just add a tiny bit of imperfection to a word? Think of vintage book covers. The letters aren’t misaligned by miles, but they have small imperfections. See the Pen Imperfection random() [forked] by @utilitybend . Here is the CSS powering the letters: @layer demo { .char { display: inline-block; /* A tiny tilt */ rotate: random(-2.8deg, 2.8deg); /* A micro nudge on X and Y */ translate: random(-1.5px, 1.5px) random(-2.8px, 2.8px); /* Very subtle ink variance */ opacity: random(0.8, 1, 0.02); transition-property: rotate, translate, opacity; transition-duration: 0.3s; transition-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1); } /* Snap straight on hover */ .word:hover .char { rotate: 0deg; translate: 0 0; opacity: 1; } } I also added a little hover effect. While you’re reading, the word feels playful. But the second you hover over it, every character snaps back. Please Don’t Break The Screen Reader One quick accessibility warning here: If you break a word into separate elements so you can style each letter, screen readers will often read it out as individual characters: “i - m - p - e - r - f - e - c - t - i - o - n”, or pause awkwardly between each one. That’s a terrible user experience. Always hide the visual spans from assistive tech and provide the full word:

i m p e r f e c t i o n

Screen reader users get the clean text, and sighted users get the fun visual quirks. Demo 2: Animating The Letters: Pure Procedural Bounce Once I had those letters sitting there with their little tilts, I couldn’t resist: what if we animated it? I started tinkering with a bounce keyframe. I was just goofing around, but the end result gave me a little smile. If you animate every letter with the exact same timing, you get that clean sine wave we’ve all seen before. But if every letter gets its own jump height, its own duration, and its own landing squash, suddenly the word looks like a bunch of little characters jumping around on a trampoline. See the Pen Bouncy imperfection with CSS random() [forked] by @utilitybend . Here is how the bounce parameters are wired up: @layer demo { .char { display: inline-block; transform-origin: center bottom; /* Procedural bounce variables */ --jump: random(element-scoped, -35px, -55px, 2px); --tilt: random(element-scoped, -8deg, 8deg, 0.5deg); --dur: random(element-scoped, 1s, 1.2s, 0.1s); --delay: random(element-scoped, -3s, 0s, 0.1s); --rebound-squash: random(element-scoped, 1.08, 1.18, 0.02); animation: letter-bounce var(--dur) linear var(--delay) infinite; } @keyframes letter-bounce { /* apex */ 0% { translate: 0 var(--jump); rotate: var(--tilt); scale: 1 1; animation-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.65, 0.05, 0.85, 0.35); } /* touchdown */ 44% { translate: 0 0; rotate: calc(var(--tilt) * 0.2); scale: 0.96 1.05; animation-timing-function: ease-out; } /* squash */ 52% { translate: 0 0; rotate: 0deg; scale: var(--rebound-squash) calc(2 - var(--rebound-squash)); animation-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1); } /* back up */ 62% { translate: 0 calc(var(--jump) * 0.2); rotate: calc(var(--tilt) * -0.4); scale: 0.98 1.03; animation-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.15, 0.85, 0.35, 1); } 100% { translate: 0 var(--jump); rotate: var(--tilt); scale: 1 1; } } } Notice the negative animation delay ( --delay: random(-3s, 0s) ). If you set a positive delay, the letters sit frozen on page load, waiting for their timers to expire before jumping. By using a negative delay, the browser pretends the animation has already been running for a few seconds. The moment the page loads, every letter is already bouncing at its own rhythm. Demo 3: Tilting Cards And Dynamic Shadows We’ve built cards. Lots of cards. So many cards... Portfolio grids, blog summaries, feature lists. And most of the time, they sit in three or four neat, boring columns. For dashboards, that’s exactly what you want. But if you’re building a lifestyle portfolio, a children’s website, or a collection of vacation photos, we can be a bit more playful. In the following example, I did just that: See the Pen Random card tilt [forked] by @utilitybend . Here’s how I put that together: @layer demo { .card { /* A gentle random tilt and vertical shift */ --tilt: random(-3.5deg, 3.5deg); --shift-y: random(-6px, 6px); rotate: var(--tilt); translate: 0 var(--shift-y); /* Shadow follows the tilt angle! */ box-shadow: calc(var(--tilt) * 1.5) calc(10px + abs(var(--tilt) * 1px)) 28px oklch(20% 0.02 260 / 0.07); transition: rotate 0.4s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1), translate 0.4s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1), box-shadow 0.4s ease; /* Straighten up on hover or keyboard focus */ &:hover, &:has(.button:focus-visible) { rotate: 0deg; translate: 0 -10px; z-index: 10; box-shadow: 0 20px 44px oklch(20% 0.02 260 / 0.12), 0 2px 6px oklch(20% 0.02 260 / 0.04); } } } In the example, playing around with the shadow was a fun experiment. I will probably try more effects with that in the future. Demo 4: The Splayed Deck With sibling-index And scroll Here is where modern CSS features start getting really interesting. In the previous demo with tilting cards, we used pure randomness. But what if you have a stack of cards that needs to fan out across the screen as you scroll? In this example, I decided to use math for the structure and randomness for the human imperfection . See the Pen Scroll drivin animations with random() tilted cards [forked] by @utilitybend . Here is the setup: @layer demo { .deck-card { position: absolute; /* Mathematical fan base via sibling-index() (centered around middle card) */ --elevation: sibling-index(); --base-rot: calc((sibling-index() - (sibling-count() + 1) / 2) * 12deg); --base-x: calc((sibling-index() - (sibling-count() + 1) / 2) * 60px); --jitter-rot: random(-3.5deg, 3.5deg); --jitter-y: random(-12px, 12px); --jitter-x: random(-8px, 8px); transform-origin: center 130%; /* SDA */ animation: splay-fan linear both; animation-timeline: scroll(root); animation-range: 0% 80%; transition: scale 0.3s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1); &:hover { scale: 1.05; /* Hovered item on top */ z-index: calc(sibling-count() + 1); } } @keyframes splay-fan { from { rotate: 0deg; translate: 0 0; box-shadow: 0 1px 3px oklch(20% 0.02 260 / 0.1), 0 2px 8px oklch(20% 0.02 260 / 0.07); } to { rotate: calc(var(--base-rot) + var(--jitter-rot)); translate: calc(var(--base-x) + var(--jitter-x)) var(--jitter-y); /* Splayed: 1. Sharp inter-card contact edge shadow 2. Elevated atmospheric shadow scaled realistically by sibling-index() */ box-shadow: 0 calc(1px + var(--elevation) * 0.6px) 4px oklch(20% 0.02 260 / 0.1), calc(var(--base-x) * 0.15) calc(10px + var(--elevation) * 5px) calc(18px + var(--elevation) * 7px) oklch(20% 0.02 260 / 0.13); } } } Look at how cleanly this works: sibling-index() calculates the mathematical fan so cards spread out evenly around the center card, and scales --elevation so cards higher in the stack cast wider shadows. calc((sibling-index() - (sibling-count() + 1) / 2) * 12deg); makes sure the amount of cards doesn’t matter; they each will rotate the same 12deg amount. random() adds the slight wobble you'd get if a person dealt the cards by hand. animation-timeline: scroll(root) ties the entire fan and shadow transition to the scrollbar. Demo 5: Random Velocity If you’ve ever looked at brutalist or high-end fashion websites, you’ve probably seen horizontal marquee text drifting across the screen as you scroll down the page. Usually, you see developers creating classes like .drift-slow , .drift-fast , .drift-reverse , or using a hefty JavaScript scroll listener to compute transforms. With random() and a tiny bit of math, we can get procedural drift speeds in just a few lines: See the Pen Random() velocity scroll animation [forked] by @utilitybend . Here is the CSS: @layer demo { .drift-line { white-space: nowrap; /* Alternate direction between rows using math parity */ --direction: calc(pow(-1, sibling-index())); /* Velocity distance */ --travel: random(15%, 44%); /* Tied to page scroll */ animation: tectonic-glide linear both; animation-timeline: scroll(root); animation-range: entry 0% cover 100%; } @keyframes tectonic-glide { from { translate: calc(var(--direction) * -1 * var(--travel)) 0; } to { translate: calc(var(--direction) * var(--travel)) 0; } } } calc(pow(-1, sibling-index())) gives us alternating directions ( 1 , -1 , 1 , -1 ), and random(15%, 44%) decides how fast each row travels. As you scroll, each typographic line moves at its own tempo. Demo 6: Blurry Randomness I love photography, and one of my favorite things about prime lenses is shallow depth of field. When you shoot at a wide aperture like f/1.7, only whatever is right on your focal plane stays sharp. Everything else melts away into soft bokeh. Yep, photography is all about that bokeh! By combining random() with filter: blur() , opacity , and scale , we can recreate that lens feel: See the Pen All about that random() bokeh [forked] by @utilitybend . Here’s the snippet: @layer demo { .focal-item { /* Random optical blur, opacity, and scale */ filter: blur(random(0px, 8px, 1px)); opacity: random(0.25, 1, 0.05); scale: random(0.85, 1.25, 0.05); transition: filter 0.4s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1), opacity 0.4s ease, scale 0.4s cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1); /* Rack-focus on hover */ &:hover, &:focus { filter: blur(0px); opacity: 1; scale: 1.15; } } } Some words land at blur(0px) with full opacity right in front of your eyes. Others blur out to 6px or 8px and fade into the background. And when you hover over any blurry item in the back, it rack-focuses right into sharpness. It’s a great little effect for decorative hero sections or tag clouds. Where Randomness Makes Sense (And Where It Doesn’t) Now that we’ve played with the wild side, let’s talk about where this actually belongs in our daily work. Good Use Cases Subtle micro-imperfection on decorative UI : Tilting polaroids, slight angles on sticky notes, or typographic hero titles. Desynchronizing ambient loops : Status beacons, gentle floating badges, or background particle grids where perfect unison looks robotic. Generative backgrounds : Star fields, confetti celebrations, floating bokeh circles, or texture grain. Editorial art direction : Magazine spreads, event flyers, brutalist layouts, and playful landing pages. Layering on top of math : Using sibling-index() for the structural grid and adding small random offsets for human warmth. Where You Should Avoid It Core layouts and grids : Don’t randomize column gutters, form field widths, or container padding. People need predictable layout geometry to navigate. Body copy : Don’t touch font sizes, line heights, or letter spacing on long-form paragraphs. Reading fatigue is real. Interactive targets : Don’t leave small buttons or links tilted or shifted without resetting them on hover and focus. If a user has to chase a moving or crooked button, you’ve failed them. But! I am happy to be proven wrong here. I encourage you to challenge the status quo and experiment with this. Always Respect prefers-reduced-motion Any time you use animations, you have to respect user preferences for reduced motion: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .char { animation: none; rotate: 0deg; translate: 0 0; } } If someone prefers reduced motion, it could also be a good idea to flatten the angles, not just the animations. I can imagine that a lot of random angles can also upset people while scrolling. Design should be fun, but never at the cost of accessibility. Wrapping My Head Around random() Tinkering with random() over the last couple of days was a lot of fun. I’m still not sure if I’ll be able to convince my designer friends, but what I do know is that it brings a bit of joy . Whenever we wanted a bit of organic randomness on the web, we had to make compromises: either pull in a JavaScript animation library, or write huge preprocessor loops that spit out hundreds of lines of static CSS. Having this built into the browser engine with zero JavaScript overhead is such a welcome addition. We spent the last decade mastering consistency, tokens, and design systems. Now that we have that foundation in place, maybe it’s time to let a little bit of playful messiness back onto the web. I really believe that the web is supposed to be fun. Never mind the defaults; here is CSS random(). See the Pen Never mind the defaults, here is css random() [forked] by @utilitybend .

items.raw_content: The Canon EOS R7 Mark II is slated for a Q1 2027 release . We haven’t anything to dispute that as of yet, so that’s what we’re rolling with. Not much has come our way in a month or so letting us know what we can expect, but that changed today when some news from a solid source hit our inbox. EOS R7 Mark II Partially Stacked Sensor? We have been told that the Canon EOS R7 Mark II will have Canon’s first EOS (as far as we know) partially stacked sensor. The source claims that a “stacked sensor” has been talked about for quite some time, but recently that changed to partially stacked. We’re writing about it because it makes a lot of sense. We imagine a partially stacked sensor would cost less to manufacture and give the added bonus of faster readout speed. I think EOS R7 Mark II customers will take the fastest readout speed that Canon can give them. Sensor Resolution We have been told numerous times that the pixel count of the sensor will go up from the EOS R7’s 32-MP pixel count, and the only resolution that we have ever heard is 39MP, or very close to it. This has always made sense to us. An EOS R7 Mark II will be a very popular camera for wildlife, sports parents, and many other uses. We think the cropping potential of a 40MP sensor will be a selling point for a large segment of shooters. Canon EOS R7 Mark II Specifications We don’t have anything to add that we’re confident in about what else to expect from the follow-up to the EOS R7, which is a high-volume camera for Canon. We think it’s safe to say that we can expect some of the features from the EOS R8 Mark II and EOS R6 Mark III will to come to the R7 II. Features like IBIS (the real version), Pre-Shooting, 40fps and it will likely be a capable video camera as well. In Closing We still believe Canon will have one more announcement date before the end of 2026, but there won’t be any new EOS R cameras coming before Q1 of next year. We have also heard a few times that Canon will announce an RF-S lens or two that will be aimed at R7 Mark II customers, aimed at R7 Mark II customers; what those lenses will be, we don’t know. It would be nice to see a super-telephoto zoom for the RF-S series and a good fast prime like the EF-M 32mm f/1.4 STM. Again, we don’t know. It seems every other manufacturer has decided to go with partially stacked sensors outside of flagship products and it’s probably time that Canon does the same thing. We also wouldn’t be surprised to see the all-new sensor make its way into higher-end Powershot cameras, but smaller than APS-C. A lot of people think the sensor in the PowerShot V1 is based on Canon’s 32.5MP APS-C sensor. We don’t have 100% confidence in the information above, but we do think it’s solid enough to write about. More to come soon.

items.raw_content: I love Italy, which I've visited a few times for both work and pleasure, and the places I've been have been pretty much what you'd expect from the tourist brochures. Gondolas. Vespas. Golden light on terracotta. Well-dressed and immaculately styled people. All present and correct. I admit, though, I've made little effort to visit the other side of the tracks. But that doesn't mean I'm not interested. And so a new show by Miron Zownir, the German-Ukrainian photographer dubbed "the poet of radical photography", definitely piqued my interest. Titled simply Italy , the exhibition takes place at Galerie Bene Taschen in Cologne, Germany. Shot across cities across the north and south of Italy, as well as rural Apulia in the south-east, these images offer a window onto Italy's many and complex social realities. If you know Zownir's work, you'll already have a good idea what that entails. If not, here's a quick primer. AIDS, arrests and a trip to Hell Born in Karlsruhe in southwestern Germany in 1953, Zownir took up photography in the late 1970s, at the height of the punk era. In 1980 he moved to the US, where he spent 15 years living in New York, LA and Pittsburgh, and his moody, expressionistic black-and-white pictures captured gay parties shortly before the AIDS crisis. Along the way he was arrested, censored and threatened more than once. Milan, 2024 (Image credit: © Miron Zownir, courtesy of Galerie Bene Taschen, Cologne) Taranto, 2024 (Image credit: © Miron Zownir, courtesy of Galerie Bene Taschen, Cologne) Florence, 2024 (Image credit: © Miron Zownir, courtesy of Galerie Bene Taschen, Cologne) In 1995 he spent three months in Moscow photographing the homeless, the dying and the dead, an experience he described as "Dante's inferno". Since then his work has hung alongside Goya, Picasso and Cindy Sherman, appeared in Fotomuseum Winterthur's Darkside exhibitions and, in 2023, placed in direct dialogue with Otto Dix at the Deichtorhallen Hamburg. So how can we summarise his Italian photos? I'd say that above all, he's seeking to capture the gap between the image the country is selling and the life its people are actually living. In Milan, a giant Dolce & Gabbana ad of a man in a wide-brimmed hat looms over an almost empty bar, with a lone drinker hunched at the counter. In Venice, a carnival reveller strides past the door of a Parisian jewellery boutique, while another frame shows a canal bridge and its lamps dissolving into fog. In Florence, Zownir shoots the famous statues of the Piazza della Signoria from below, turning Hercules into a muscular black silhouette against the clouds, David reduced to a bystander. In Taranto, he finds a crumbling palazzo with huge eyes staring out from its empty window frames across a deserted square. Venice, 2024 (Image credit: © Miron Zownir, courtesy of Galerie Bene Taschen, Cologne) Venice, 2024 (Image credit: © Miron Zownir, courtesy of Galerie Bene Taschen, Cologne) Milan, 2024 (Image credit: © Miron Zownir, courtesy of Galerie Bene Taschen, Cologne) It's not all grim and negative, though. For instance, a shot of a young woman in Milan, all face piercings and leg tattoos, reflects the fascination with people outside the mainstream he's had since his punk days. Indeed, Zownir himself would bristle at the idea that he's only interested in gloom. "What you might consider dark or grotesque might well be free, uncompromising, strange, tragic, unique, interesting or whatever," he once told Slow Travel Berlin . On this evidence, Italy has plenty of all of the above. Italy runs at Galerie Bene Taschen , Lindenstrasse 19, Cologne, Germany, from Saturday, November 28, 2pm-6pm until Saturday, February 6.

In this episode of the No Film School Podcast , director Georgia Oakley joins No Film School's GG Hawkins to discuss her new adaptation, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the Dashwood sisters. Oakley shares how she approached the film through the lens of sisterhood, longing, and the timeless tension between women's expectations and societal constraints. She breaks down her filmmaking process, from shooting on 35mm film and using two cameras to capture authentic performances to collaborating with cinematographers Arnaud Potier and Tasha Back on naturalistic visuals. items.raw_content: Did the headline pull you in? I hope so; that was my intent, because I am here to tell you that the penis in this landmark documentary is maybe the most essential part of it; the penis tells the whole story of Elizabeth Holmes. If you haven't seen You Can See Everything , go watch it. It's amazing. This article will be all spoilers. If you have, you know that about forty minutes into the movie, judging by my internal clock, we get a workout montage featuring Elizabeth Holmes's husband, Billy Evans. Then, Billy steps into the shower to wash off, and we see him fully naked as he washes himself off. This is literally a tie-in to the title, but this naked sharing of their lives also becomes a metaphor for the story, an emasculation of the directors, and a hubristic trap Evans himself falls into. Yes, the whole theme of the movie is tied up in one penis. Let's dive in. - YouTube www.youtube.com You Can Literally See Everything In most documentaries, you're not getting full-frontal male nudity. In fact, I don't think I have seen many docs with any nudity at all. They're usually pretty scholarly, and even ones about salacious things pick and choose when to show someone naked. Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything also makes careful, calculated decisions about what it shows and when it shows it to you. So getting a penis early in the movie is something they decided to do in the edit. They could have left it out, so I want to explore why it's here, why it's so early, and what it means for the characters. This movie is three hours long and split into two parts, with perspective shifts that recontextualize what we have seen, like a magic trick. This is a tale as old as time in docs, first seen in Orson Welles's F is for Fake and later used in docs like The Act of Killing to illustrate a point. Here, Fielder and Oppenheim use that strategy to turn our judgment of Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans. But the only way to do that is to show them, naked, in the first half as the people they claim to be. That it is both literal and metaphorical. One from the living with the subjects sense, and the other from seeing a penis in the shower. Enter: actual nudity from Billy Evans post-workout. At the time, we just think this is a quirky thing from a guy who is proud of his body, a narcissist who is leaning way too slowly into the "We're innocent, we'll show you anything you want and let you examine our lives to any degree to prove it." But as we get deeper into the film, we recontextualize this nudity as narcissism and toxic masculinity. Something planted early on, when we see him yank the omelet away from his wife and tell her she whips the eggs wrong. In both instances, we have plants that pay off later, showing how physical exposure (both penis and egg power) can function as psychological warfare, and how they connect only when you reveal a person's true motive. Since we have the motives early on, as the toxicity shows itself later, we can harken back to both the dick and the omelet as precursors to us hitting that this story would be about a power swing. In this movie, Billy's true motive is seen as control. The big question becomes: how much of that control does Elizabeth cede to avoid charges, and how much is she actually being taken advantage of by a man pushing her around? 'You Can See Everything' Credit: A24 The Power Dynamic Behind the Exposure According to co-director Lance Oppenheim, the nudity moment early in the movie wasn't either director's idea. Evans offered to let the crew film him in the shower, claiming he had zero problems about being seen naked. So, they obliged. To Evans, exposure is leverage. On paper, his bizarre justification for showing his body on camera is that displaying his penis somehow serves as absolute proof of his wife’s innocence. It’s a delusion wrapped in pseudo-logic, but it also exposes that Billy just wants to dominate everyone around him. This guy is showing his penis to use his own body as an instrument of intimidation. It's a way of showing the documentarian he's the alpha in the room, and their cameras can only capture him succeeding. This is Billy Evans's attempt to assert a twisted form of hyper-masculinity, designed to emasculate the directors behind the lens. It's a classic power play, converting raw exposure into a literal flex. And somehow, Fielder and Oppenheim keep their composure enough to include it in the movie, which lets them have all the power later. Billy can't conceive of them having any power, because he doesn't see these two funny directors as guys with power. But he's wrong; beneath the surface, they have all the power, not just in the edit, but in the ability to edit a movie with hindsight. They can harken back to his penis and say...why show us that? Who are you really? Something he's not smart enough to understand. This all makes the penis necessary, and the whole crux of the movie, as they all dance around the Holmes accusations and portray different versions of the same story, allowing the audience to decide her innocence. For directors and editors, the scene offers a brilliant study in how subject agency can reveal character faster than any interview dialogue ever could. Fielder and Oppenheim turn Evans' attempt at emasculation on its head. The moment stops being a display of male dominance and becomes a staggering portrait of self-delusion. It's truly one of the bravest acts of documentary directing and one of the funniest things, to see this blowhard's big penis backfire on him so completely that you walk out of the documentary talking about how dumb this big dicked idiot looks on screen. The Takeaway for Directors Yes, there are lessons in all of this, and the directors set them. When you make a doc, you can find the underlying truth in the edit, and I think in You Can See Everything , they found it later when they saw Billy's true colors. When they set up the movie, you get the nudity early, which jars many viewers; only later do you realize what it's for, and only then do you feel it. So, when your subject tries to hijack your camera to project power, sometimes the most honest choice a filmmaker can make is to let them do it, holding the shot until the performance exposes itself. You have that; you can share it with the world. That's what makes this one of the greatest documentaries of all time, and I think a movie is also a piece of modern art. Let me know what you think in the comments.

items.raw_content: In Coca-Cola's latest campaign, four independent business owners get something usually reserved for kings and queens: an oil-on-canvas portrait by artists who've sat opposite the late Queen, King Charles and Princess Anne. Before the camera came along, only the very rich could afford to have themselves immortalised in oils. I'm talking royalty, aristocrats, and the odd wealthy merchant; their portraits often hang in prestigious galleries or National Trust properties. Their noble gazes in gilt frames suggest a life of privilege, while everyone else went undocumented. Even today, a formal portrait remains a status symbol. So it's quite unusual to find a portrait of the person who serves you chips on a Saturday night. But that's what's happened in a new campaign by Coca-Cola. The drinks brand has commissioned four of Britain's finest portrait artists, each of whom has painted an official portrait of a member of the Royal Family, to paint a fish-and-chip shop owner, a café proprietor, a pub landlord and a corner shop owner. The finished works will be on show at London's Saatchi Gallery from today until 1 November, and admission is free. It's the latest chapter in Coca-Cola's 'Localness' platform, which celebrates the people behind the pubs, shops and cafés where its drinks are served. It follows last year's documentary and photo series, The Bosses, and Counter Cultures earlier in 2026. This time around, the campaign borrows the visual language of official portraiture. And we love it. Because why shouldn't a Barnsley chippy get the same gravitas as Buckingham Palace? Pindy Kaur by Nicky Philipps Simon Dafforn-Jones by Jamie Coreth Everyone else seems to agree. New research commissioned by Coca-Cola Great Britain found that 79% of people think independent businesses are under-appreciated, while 80% want to see them celebrated more often. "Independent business owners create the places where local life happens, yet their contribution often goes unrecognised," says Rhona Stephen, senior director of communications for Coca-Cola Great Britain. "With Local Royalty, we wanted to celebrate them in a way that felt deliberately unexpected and enduring. By borrowing the visual language of official portraiture and placing these owners at its centre, the campaign gives their everyday impact the status it deserves." So who got their portrait done? First up is Pindy Kaur, who took over a struggling Ocean Fish Bar in Barnsley in the 1990s. More than 25 years on, she and her family have turned it into a much-loved takeaway, known for its regulars and its family-run spirit. Pindy is a devoted admirer of the late Queen Elizabeth II, and she was painted by Nicky Philipps, who painted the Queen not once but twice. Gino Verecchia by Gareth Reid Kaual Patel by Nick Bashall Gino Verecchia's University Café in Glasgow was opened by his grandfather, Pasquale, in 1918, and it's been in the family for three generations. Wow. It blends Italian heritage (including a 100-year-old gelato recipe) with Scottish favourites, and it's a true Glasgow institution. It even once served Anthony Bourdain battered haggis. Gareth Reid, portrait artist to King Charles III when he was Prince of Wales, painted Gino. Down in Dittisham, South Devon, meanwhile, The Ferry Boat Inn sits on the banks of the River Dart. Locals know it as the FBI. Brilliant. Landlord Simon Dafforn-Jones, or "Slugger" to the locals, has run it for almost 20 years, following in his dad's footsteps. He gives local teens their first jobs and champions produce from across the region, so the pub naturally sits at the heart of village life. He was painted by Jamie Coreth, who created the first official portrait of the Prince and Princess of Wales. And finally, Kaual Patel's father bought Torridon Convenience Store in Catford, South East London, in 1984, and Kaual took over in 2000. Over the past two decades, he has made it a real community hub, stocking local producers alongside the bigger household names. His mantra is lovely: "If you're a local producer, there's a space on my shelf for you." Kaual was painted by Nick Bashall, portrait painter to Princess Anne. Kaual Patel by Nick Bashall Gino Verecchia by Gareth Reid Pindy Kaur by Nicky Philipps Simon Dafforn-Jones by Jamie Coreth There you have it. All worthy contenders. All beautifully depicted. Alongside their finished portraits, the Saatchi show includes behind-the-scenes footage from the sittings. It shows how each artist got to know their sitter and turned their character and history into a formal portrait. Each owner also donates to a local charity of their choice and keeps the portrait to hang in their home or business. MHP Group created and delivered the campaign across MHP, Mischief and Studio La Plage. Find out more on Coca-Cola's website . So next time you're enjoying a pint or picking up a chippy tea, take a moment to appreciate the people behind the counter. You might be in the presence of royalty.

items.title: Accordion Icons: Which Work Best?
items.summary_what: Accordion Icons: Which Work Best?: So what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions?

items.raw_content: So what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions? Is there really any noticeable difference between carets, chevrons, arrows, and triangles? Well, research shows that there is some difference indeed. But what’s more interesting is that split menus are harmful , why it's better to not have icons and text labels link to different actions, and why the caret is the safest icon choice. Let’s dive in! No Icon = Opening The Page The findings aren’t very surprising: without any icon in use, users expect that tapping on the menu item would take them directly to a new page. Users often struggle with custom icons as they don't clearly signal that they'll open an accordion. And people tend to tap fairly equally on the icon and on the label for most icons. Many designs (like the one below) tend to slightly overcomplicate things by adding arrows and carets pointing everywhere, depending on the state of the accordion. But typically we don't need to use an arrow to indicate a link to the category. The rule of thumb is very simple: if it’s a link, the easiest and most effective way is to simply underline it — without any arrow, caret, or other icon. Perhaps it’s not particularly exciting, but it works flawlessly every single time. Confusing Behavior With Arrows ▶ and Split Buttons Using a right-facing arrow icon ▶ isn’t associated with an expectation of going directly to a new page. And having the same icon pointing down ▼ doesn’t necessarily imply that an accordion is going to open on tap/click. It’s a good idea to avoid split buttons for accordions — where the text label links directly to a page, but the icon opens the accordion. Instead, it’s much more reliable to allow users to tap on a main category and expose the menu; and to access the category page, we add a link to it inside the menu. Plus +/− and Arrows ↓/↑ Are Understood, But Can Be Misunderstood For accordions, we typically use +/− or arrows ↓/↑ to signal expanded and collapsed states, and typically it works well. However, both have many different interpretations . Plus + can mean anything from saving for later to adding to cart to zooming in, and can be particularly confusing for multi-level navigation, with many levels open at the same time. Arrows ↓/↑ can mean scrolling or sliding or finding the next match, but also a jump to a particular portion of a page. Both plus and arrows are well-understood and work, but depending on the design, can be confusing — mostly because they are overloaded . Wrapping Up The safe choice is to use the caret/triangle pointing down ▼ by default , and change it to a caret pointing up or a caret pointing sideways ▶ on interaction. If you need an alternative, then +/- typically work well, too. But we certainly don’t need any further icons or arrows to indicate where the links go. The same goes for split menus, which often produce more mistakes than help. Instead, we have one button or dropdown that does exactly one thing — shows all options and allows users to drill down. And if you need a direct link, we link the title directly to the page and underline it . More often than not, simpler is better. items.title: Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?
items.summary_what: Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?: The way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy.
items.summary_why: Influences typography, UI/UX prototyping speed, and vector design production assets.

items.raw_content: The way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy. If it were turned into a movie, reviewers would say it was unbelievable. Nobody could be that stupid. Yet here we are. And what makes it all the more frustrating is that we have been here before . Back in 2014, I wrote a book for Smashing Magazine called Digital Adaptation , looking at the mistakes being made in how organizations were approaching digital transformation and what they should be doing instead. The similarities between then and now are striking. So in this post, I want to look back at Digital Adaptation and see how the lessons in that book apply to the AI era and what we can learn from the past to help us navigate the challenges of AI today. The biggest mistake, both then and now, is approaching each as a technological challenge. It’s About People, Not Technology Sure, both digital transformation and AI are technological advances, and yes, some level of technological implementation is required. But that is the tip of a very large iceberg. Back in the midst of the digital transformation era, IT departments were rolling out CMSs, CRM systems, intranets, and so on. Meanwhile, on the customer-facing side, organizations were rolling out websites, apps, and personalization. But they were putting almost no emphasis on how people were going to use these systems. Internal systems were hard to use, and customers either didn’t care what was being built or wanted something else entirely. The same is happening with AI. Senior management are buying into the hype, and IT teams are rolling out Copilot Studio licenses company-wide and considering the job done. Sure, there is a bit of organization-wide generic training, but that’s about it. Just like before, staff are left wondering what to do with these new systems and feeling under pressure to use them and deliver results. Organizations need to recognize that AI is a cultural shift as much as a technology , and that shift has enormous implications for their staff. After all, this time around, it is even worse, because this time, staff fear for their jobs. They have read the same headlines that you have, and no amount of promises from senior management is going to make them feel any better. Why Would Staff Want To Adopt AI? I mean, think about it from a staff member’s point of view. AI offers them very little personally, even setting aside the fact that management may be intending to use it to replace them. The main reason senior management are excited about AI is that it provides additional productivity . People can do more in less time. But that does not benefit staff. They are still required to work 9 to 5, but now they are expected to do more in the same time. They don’t get any time back, and they don’t get paid more, so why would they embrace AI? So before asking staff to embrace AI, organizations need to ask themselves how they intend to motivate them to do so. One strategy is to help staff identify the parts of their job they hate and how AI can help them do those tasks more quickly and less painfully. People tend to be a lot more receptive to change when it is presented as an opportunity to improve their working lives . But, that should just be the beginning. Organizations may need to consider providing incentives for staff to adopt AI in terms of career progression, compensation, or shorter working hours. Staff Need Time And Support To Adopt AI Also, adopting AI is not a simple task. It involves challenging every working practice they have built up over (in some cases) decades. All of that procedural knowledge has to be rebuilt. That is a lot to ask of anybody in even the best of circumstances, and most employees do not find themselves in the best of circumstances. Most are overworked and struggling to stay on top of their to-do lists. They don’t have time to sit down, learn a new tool, and figure out how it fits into their workflow. That doesn’t just take time. It also takes a lot of consideration and experimentation . It is not enough to just send a member of staff on a training course and expect them to be able to use AI to its full potential. At a minimum, staff need training specific to their roles, such as the AI training I provide to UX teams . But organizations should be going even further. They need to develop sophisticated training programs that help staff from different departments understand how to use AI in their specific roles. They need ongoing support and the time to experiment with AI to find the best ways to use it. But formal training will only take you so far. In my experience, the most effective support comes from colleagues , which is why I would start with the enthusiasts rather than the resisters. Every organization has a handful of people who are already experimenting with AI, often without anybody asking them to. Bring those people together, give them the time and space to share what is working for them, and let their enthusiasm spread to everyone else. I saw this work during the digital transformation era too. In Digital Adaptation , I described an internal conference where staff showed their colleagues what they had built, and it did more for adoption than any memo from the top ever could. People are far more likely to try something when they see a colleague in a similar role using it successfully than when they are told to by senior management. Rather than trying to win over the most resistant staff first, organizations should find the people already experimenting with AI, give them time to share what they have learned, and let social proof do the heavy lifting. Unfortunately, experimentation comes with a big downside… mistakes will be made. It Needs To Be Safe To Fail Many organizations have, to be frank, a culture of fear where mistakes are seen as a sign of incompetence. However, by its very nature, learning a new tool like AI will involve making mistakes, and this can be a massive barrier to adoption. I saw this during the era of digital transformation. Senior management would demand digital transformation and were confused when it didn’t happen. What they didn’t realize was that they were sending mixed messages to staff. Sure, they were asking for digital transformation, but they were still demanding that the same key performance indicators (KPIs) be met, and they still pointed out any mistakes in their annual reviews. There was no space to fail , as the pressure to deliver was relentless. This time around, it seems to be even worse. I hear horror stories of staff being reprimanded for using too many tokens just weeks after being told to adopt AI. Or staff being lectured so much about what they should or should not do with AI that they are afraid to try anything. It is safer to just do what they have always done. If management want staff to adopt AI, then they need to make staff feel safe to experiment . They need to adjust KPIs, change how staff are reviewed, and relax some of the governance while staff are learning. Handle Governance With Care Look, I get it. AI cannot be rolled out without some governance in place, but again, this is an area that organizations have typically handled poorly. In the midst of digital transformation, governance would either be non-existent, or it would be so strict that it would stifle innovation, and unfortunately, I see the same pattern emerging with AI adoption. Staff need some governance to help them know where they stand. It helps them understand what is expected of them and what they can and cannot do. But too often organizations have been so strict that it is easier not to do anything at all. Pages of instructions about what people should and should not share with AI create that sense of fear that I mentioned earlier. Organizations need a short set of principles that would fit on a handful of posters, similar to gov.uk’s design principles . Beyond that, they need to demonstrate a degree of trust in their staff to use common sense. Of course, mistakes will get made, but that is the cost of change, and so organizations need to accept that and do what they can to mitigate that in how they roll out the technology. Adaptive Technological Rollout That said, organizations will need to be careful in how they roll out AI from an IT perspective. Once again, it is easy to lock everything down and stifle the adoption of AI. Again, this is something I highlighted back in 2014 with digital transformation. Overstretched IT teams would pick a set of technologies and roll them out organization-wide, often with little or no consultation with the individuals who would be using them. Anything outside of that set of technologies had to go through a complex approval process, normally involving a steering committee. The result was a glacial pace of change that was one of the major contributing factors to the failure rate of digital transformation projects. Today we are seeing the same thing. IT teams are opting into a tool like Copilot and calling it a day, but that often falls massively short. Take, for example, a UX team I am working with at the moment. Management is pushing hard for AI adoption, and the team is excited about the potential of creating an AI-powered research repository and even AI personas. It sounds like a wonderful case study in AI adoption, with enthusiastic management, an excited team, and innovative ideas. Unfortunately, the reality is that nothing is happening because Copilot cannot deliver on the team’s vision, and so they are currently bogged down in bureaucracy as they try to persuade the AI steering group that they need to use a different toolset. Understandably, the team’s enthusiasm is waning. Why bother? And that team is one of the more patient ones. In many organizations, staff are not waiting for the steering group at all. Just as we saw shadow IT during the digital transformation era, with people signing up for Dropbox and Google Docs because the official tools could not do what they needed, we are now seeing shadow AI. When the in-house AI tool will not let people do their jobs, they open a personal ChatGPT or Claude account on their phone or home laptop and get on with it. That is far more dangerous than the problem the restrictions were meant to prevent. Company data ends up in tools the organization has no control over, with no oversight and no record of what has been shared. In trying to lock everything down, organizations end up pushing the risk somewhere they cannot see it. The instinctive reaction is to clamp down with stricter policies, blocked websites, and warnings about disciplinary action. But that rarely works, and it drives the behavior further underground. Shadow AI is a symptom , and a useful one, because it shows exactly where the official tools are falling short. Instead of trying to stamp out shadow AI, organizations should learn from it. Talk to staff about what they are using personal accounts for and what they feel they cannot do with the AI they have been given, then use that to shape what gets rolled out next. Look, I understand the cost of a messy, out-of-control tech stack. It is not ideal. However, in the early days of adoption, we may have to live with a bit of chaos while people explore the edges of what is possible and work out common use cases. Organizations need to allow staff to explore different uses of AI and even different AI apps to find what suits their specific needs in their specific roles. They can always start locking things down later as the real organizational needs become clearer. A Dangerous Time I admit all of this feels dangerous to some organizations. They want to control the AI adoption process centrally and make sure nothing goes wrong. I understand that. But change comes with a degree of risk, and the risk of moving too slowly is greater than the risk of moving too fast. However, a bigger danger still is when organizations see this as a technological challenge and overlook the human side of things. AI adoption is not simply about rolling out new technology. Just like digital transformation, it is about people , culture , and change management . The sooner organizations realize the scope of what they are dealing with, the better.
